provenance.rightsNote: Lectio Edition (SDIT): clear modern English of Machiavelli's The Prince, synthesized from the public-domain translation tradition (Marriott 1908; Thomson 1882) and checked against the Italian; modern translations consulted, not quoted. In progress, chapter by chapter.
sourcesCited: Italian, the original text of Il Principe
W. K. Marriott, The Prince (1908, public domain)

character: Plain modern English — the sense of the original, made to read with ease today.
overview: The Lectio Edition renders Machiavelli's The Prince in plain modern English that keeps its cold clarity and bite — how power is won, held, and lost; fortune and virtù; cruelty and mercy weighed as instruments — without the antique stiffness.
introduction: The Prince is a short, shocking handbook on power, written by an out-of-work diplomat hoping to win back a place in Medici Florence. It sets aside how rulers ought to behave for how they actually must, if they mean to keep their state. Bracing, unsentimental, and still argued over five centuries later.

divergences.phrase: o per fortuna o per virtù
divergences.older: or else by fortune or by ability (Marriott)
divergences.lectio: either by fortune or by virtù — a man's own skill and nerve
divergences.note: Virtù is the load-bearing word of the whole book — skill, force, and daring fused into one quality, with no moral content at all. Marriott dissolves it into a different English word at each occurrence ('ability' here, 'valour' and 'energy' elsewhere), which hides the fact that Machiavelli is running a single argument on a single term. The Lectio keeps the Italian word throughout, glossed once at this first use.

divergences.phrase: non ha sostenuto li assalti... per altre cagioni che per essere antiquato in quello dominio
divergences.older: who could not have withstood the attacks of the Venetians in '84, nor those of Pope Julius in '10, unless he had been long established in his dominions (Marriott)
divergences.lectio: held out against the assaults of the Venetians in '84, and of Pope Julius in '10, for no other reason than that his house was old in that dominion
divergences.note: The Italian states a fact, not a hypothesis: the Duke did survive both attacks, and the age of his dynasty was the only reason. Marriott's counterfactual ('could not have... unless') is logically equivalent but softens the flat, diagnostic tone — Machiavelli reads results backward to causes, like an autopsy.

divergences.phrase: sempre una mutazione lascia lo addentellato per la edificazione dell'altra
divergences.older: one change always leaves the toothing for another (Marriott)
divergences.lectio: one change always leaves jutting brickwork for the next to build on
divergences.note: Addentellato is a mason's term: the toothed course of bricks left projecting from a wall so the next stretch can be bonded to it. Marriott's 'toothing' is the correct trade word but opaque to most readers now; the Lectio unpacks the image instead, because the image is the point — every revolution leaves a ready-made anchor for the one after it.

divergences.phrase: che sieno quasi compedes di quello stato
divergences.older: which may be as keys to that state (Marriott)
divergences.lectio: that will serve as shackles on that state
divergences.note: The manuscripts read compedes — Latin for leg-irons. Marriott follows the softer reading found in some printed texts, le chiavi, 'keys.' But colonies here are not a way in; they are restraints locked onto a conquered province to keep it from moving. The harder reading is Machiavelli's, and it is the colder image.

divergences.phrase: li uomini si debbano o vezzeggiare o spegnere
divergences.older: men ought either to be well treated or crushed (Marriott)
divergences.lectio: men should be either treated well or snuffed out
divergences.note: Spegnere is to put out a flame — and it is the verb Machiavelli reaches for again and again when a bloodline, a memory, or a republic must be eliminated. 'Snuffed out' keeps the image and the chill, and the Lectio renders the verb the same way at every recurrence, so the reader can hear the maxim echo through the book.

divergences.phrase: godere el benefizio del tempo... ma sì bene quello della virtù e prudenzia loro
divergences.older: Let us enjoy the benefits of the time — but rather the benefits of their own valour and prudence (Marriott)
divergences.lectio: enjoy the benefit of time. They preferred the benefit of their own virtù and prudence
divergences.note: Marriott's 'valour' narrows virtù to battlefield courage. Here it is the whole Roman quality — foresight, energy, initiative, force — set directly against waiting for time and fortune to sort things out. That opposition, virtù versus fortuna, is the spine of the book, so the Lectio keeps the word.

divergences.phrase: non è nato dalla poca o molta virtù del vincitore, ma dalla disformità del subietto
divergences.older: this is not occasioned by the little or abundance of ability in the conqueror, but by the want of uniformity in the subject state (Marriott)
divergences.lectio: it comes not from the little or great virtù of the conqueror, but from the difference in what was conquered
divergences.note: The chapter's cold conclusion: outcomes are structural, not personal. Keeping virtù makes the point unmistakable — even the conqueror's defining quality is beside the point when the material he conquers is built differently. Marriott's 'ability' loses the deliberate shock of setting the book's hero-word aside.

divergences.phrase: non li potendo né contentare né spegnere
divergences.older: as you are unable either to satisfy or exterminate them (Marriott)
divergences.lectio: being able neither to satisfy them nor to snuff them out
divergences.note: Spegnere again — the extinguishing verb from Chapter III's maxim about treating men well or snuffing them out. Marriott varies it ('crushed' there, 'exterminate' here); the Lectio keeps one English verb for it so the reader hears Machiavelli applying the same rule, in the same words, to a new case.

divergences.phrase: creandovi drento uno stato di pochi
divergences.older: establishing within it an oligarchy (Marriott)
divergences.lectio: setting up inside a government of a few men
divergences.note: Machiavelli writes plain Italian — uno stato di pochi, 'a state of the few' — not the Greek political term. Marriott's 'oligarchy' classicizes what is meant as a flat piece of machinery: a small client government, made by the prince and owned by him, that cannot survive without him. The Lectio keeps the phrasing instrumental.

divergences.phrase: tanto che la più sicura via è spegnerle o abitarvi
divergences.older: so that the safest way is to destroy them or to reside there (Marriott)
divergences.lectio: So the safest way is to snuff them out — or to go and live there
divergences.note: The chapter closes on spegnere, the extinguishing verb of Chapter III's maxim, now applied to whole republics. Rendering it identically lets the ending land as the maxim scaled up: two options, priced like a bill of costs, with the flame image intact under the bookkeeping.

divergences.phrase: virtù
divergences.older: ability
divergences.lectio: virtù
divergences.note: Marriott renders Machiavelli's keyword as 'ability' (elsewhere 'valour', 'powers', 'genius'), which flattens it. Virtù is the book's central term of art — skill, force, nerve, timing, everything in a man that is not luck — and it is pointedly not moral virtue. English has no single word for it, so the Lectio keeps the Italian, here and throughout.

divergences.phrase: ne renda qualche odore
divergences.older: at least it will savour of it
divergences.lectio: at least it carries some scent of it
divergences.note: Machiavelli's metaphor for imitation is smell: walk close enough behind great men and some aroma of their greatness clings to you. Marriott's 'savour' has gone quaint; 'scent' keeps the trace-of-greatness image a modern reader can actually smell.

divergences.phrase: lo fece mettere in dua pezzi in su la piazza
divergences.older: caused him to be executed and left on the piazza at Cesena with the block and a bloody knife at his side
divergences.lectio: one morning at Cesena he had Ramiro laid out in two pieces on the piazza, with a block of wood and a bloody knife beside him
divergences.note: Marriott softens the most notorious image in the book into a routine execution. The Italian says exactly what the crowd saw: the body cut in two. Machiavelli reports it without a flicker, and the sentence's cold precision is the whole effect — the Lectio restores what Borgia actually put on display.

divergences.phrase: satisfatti e stupidi
divergences.older: satisfied and dismayed
divergences.lectio: satisfied and stunned
divergences.note: Stupidi is 'stupefied' — struck dumb — not 'dismayed.' Machiavelli is coolly measuring the effect of a piece of political theater, not registering the people's disapproval. The pairing is the point: the spectacle worked on both registers at once.

divergences.phrase: acquistò lo stato con la fortuna del padre e con quella lo perdé
divergences.older: acquired his state during the ascendancy of his father, and on its decline he lost it
divergences.lectio: acquired his state by his father's fortune and lost it the same way
divergences.note: The Italian sentence rides a single word — fortuna — in and out: what fortune gave, fortune took. Marriott's paraphrase ('ascendancy... decline') explains the history but loses the balance that makes it an epigram, and with it the chapter's thesis in miniature.

divergences.phrase: crudeltà male usate o bene usate
divergences.older: severities being badly or properly used
divergences.lectio: cruelties badly used or well used
divergences.note: Marriott flinches twice — 'severities' for cruelties, 'properly' for well — and his own footnote admits 'crudeltà' means more than that. The phrase is deliberately shocking in its bookkeeping calm: Machiavelli grades cruelty like a technique. The Lectio keeps the ice.

divergences.phrase: Non si può ancora chiamare virtù ammazzare li sua cittadini
divergences.older: Yet it cannot be called talent to slay fellow-citizens
divergences.lectio: And yet it cannot be called virtù to kill your fellow citizens
divergences.note: This is the one sentence where Machiavelli polices his own keyword — Agathocles has every quality virtù names, and still the word is refused him: such methods win empire, not glory. Marriott's 'talent' makes it a remark about aptitude and loses the shock of the withheld term.

divergences.phrase: tu non se' a tempo al male, e il bene che tu fai non ti giova
divergences.older: you are too late for harsh measures; and mild ones will not help you
divergences.lectio: you are too late for the evil, and the good you do buys you nothing
divergences.note: Machiavelli writes male and bene — evil and good, flat and unmoralized, as instruments with expiration dates. Marriott's 'harsh measures and mild ones' turns a moral shock into administrative vocabulary and hides that the book has just called cruelty by its name.

divergences.phrase: dua umori diversi
divergences.older: these two distinct parties are found
divergences.lectio: these two opposed humors are found in every city
divergences.note: Machiavelli's metaphor is medical: a city has humors the way a body does, and politics is what happens when they clash — the same word he uses elsewhere for the ailments of states. Marriott's 'parties' dissolves the diagnosis into modern party politics, which is exactly what it is not.

divergences.phrase: o principato o libertà o licenzia
divergences.older: either a principality, self-government, or anarchy
divergences.lectio: principality, liberty, or license
divergences.note: The triad is exact: one-man rule, free self-rule, and licenzia — liberty curdled into lawlessness. 'Anarchy' isn't wrong, but 'license' keeps the third term as the disease-form of the second, which is the whole logic of the sentence.

divergences.phrase: astuzia fortunata
divergences.older: a happy shrewdness
divergences.lectio: a kind of lucky cunning
divergences.note: Machiavelli coins a hybrid for the civil prince: not virtù, not fortune, but cunning that got lucky — a faintly backhanded compliment. 'Happy shrewdness' has gone soft with age; 'lucky cunning' keeps both the craft and the luck, and the slight edge of neither being quite enough alone.

divergences.phrase: da vivere, bere e ardere per uno anno
divergences.older: enough for one year's eating, drinking, and firing
divergences.lectio: enough in the public stores to eat, drink, and burn for a year
divergences.note: 'Firing' meant fuel in 1908 and now reads as gunnery. Machiavelli's triplet is a quartermaster's list — groceries and firewood — and its plainness is the point: the German cities are unafraid because their pantries are full.

divergences.phrase: quando non li manchi né da vivere né da difendersi
divergences.older: when he does not fail to support and defend them
divergences.lectio: so long as they lack neither food nor the means to fight
divergences.note: The chapter's closing condition is logistical, not sentimental: the citizens hold firm while supplies and arms hold out. Marriott turns stock-keeping into paternal care — the prince supporting his people — and blunts the cold arithmetic the whole chapter runs on.

divergences.phrase: si acquistano o per virtù o per fortuna, e sanza l'una e l'altra si mantengano
divergences.older: they are acquired either by capacity or good fortune, and they can be held without either
divergences.lectio: they are acquired by virtù or by fortune, and kept without either
divergences.note: Marriott dissolves Machiavelli's signature word virtù into 'capacity.' The Lectio edition keeps virtù untranslated throughout — it means ability, nerve, force of character, not moral virtue — because the whole book turns on it. Church states are Machiavelli's one deadpan exception: the only principalities that require none of it.

divergences.phrase: Svizzeri sono armatissimi e liberissimi
divergences.older: The Switzers are completely armed and quite free.
divergences.lectio: The Swiss are the best-armed people alive, and the freest.
divergences.note: Machiavelli makes the argument in two superlatives: most armed, most free — cause and effect in four words. Marriott's 'quite free' deflates the second one, and 'Switzers' is an antique demonym. We restore both superlatives at full pressure and call the Swiss what modern readers call them.

divergences.phrase: tenerlo con le leggi, che non passi el segno
divergences.older: to hold him by the laws so that he does not leave the command
divergences.lectio: bind him with laws so that he does not overstep the mark
divergences.note: Machiavelli's worry is not that a winning citizen-general will desert his post but that he will grow past it — 'che non passi el segno,' that he not cross the line. Marriott has the republic keeping its captain at work; the Italian has it keeping him on a leash.

divergences.phrase: ne' mercennarii è più pericolosa la ignavia, nelli ausiliarii, la virtù
divergences.older: in mercenaries dastardy is most dangerous; in auxiliaries, valour
divergences.lectio: with mercenaries the deadliest thing is their cowardice; with auxiliaries, their virtù
divergences.note: The epigram turns on virtù: the very quality the whole book prizes becomes lethal the moment it belongs to someone else's army. Marriott's 'valour' keeps the paradox but loses the echo; keeping the word lets the reader hear it snap shut.

divergences.phrase: Colui adunque che vuole non potere vincere, si vaglia di queste armi
divergences.older: Therefore, let him who has no desire to conquer make use of these arms
divergences.lectio: So: the man who wants to make sure he cannot win should use these arms
divergences.note: The Italian is colder than 'no desire to conquer.' Machiavelli says 'wants to be unable to win' — not weak motivation but engineered impossibility, ruin by design. We keep the sarcasm at full strength.

divergences.phrase: se noi volessimo ritirarci, come aremmo a fare? se loro si ritirassino, come aremmo a seguirli?
divergences.older: If we should wish to retreat, how ought we to pursue?
divergences.lectio: If we wanted to retreat, how would we manage it? If they retreated, how should we pursue?
divergences.note: Marriott telescopes two of Philopoemen's field questions into one impossible sentence — retreating and pursuing at once. The Italian asks them separately: our retreat, then theirs. We restore both questions.

divergences.phrase: andare drieto alla verità effettuale della cosa, che alla imaginazione di essa
divergences.older: more appropriate to follow up the real truth of the matter than the imagination of it
divergences.lectio: more fitting to go straight after the effectual truth of the thing than after the imagination of it
divergences.note: Verità effettuale — truth measured by effects, the truth of what actually works — is Machiavelli's own coinage and the hinge of the whole book: the sentence where political thought breaks with every mirror-for-princes before it. Marriott's 'real truth' flattens the coinage into ordinary emphasis; we keep its strangeness, because the strangeness is the point.

divergences.phrase: imparare a potere essere non buono
divergences.older: to know how to do wrong
divergences.lectio: to learn how not to be good
divergences.note: Marriott moralizes. Machiavelli does not say 'do wrong' — he says the prince must learn 'to be able to be not good': a capacity, held in reserve, switched on and off as necessity requires. The negative construction is the scandal of the sentence, and we keep it.

divergences.phrase: conviene rovini infra tanti che non sono buoni
divergences.older: soon meets with what destroys him among so much that is evil
divergences.lectio: must come to ruin among so many who are not good
divergences.note: The Italian ends on people, not abstraction: 'among so many who are not good.' Marriott's 'so much that is evil' turns the crowd into a fog of wickedness; Machiavelli is counting his neighbors — and note he calls them 'not good,' the same cool phrase he has just prescribed for the prince.

divergences.phrase: né può essere questo esemplo più miserabile né più raro
divergences.older: nor could there be a more admirable example, nor one more rare
divergences.lectio: no example could be more wretched, or more rare
divergences.note: A textual crux: some copies of the Italian read mirabile (admirable), the modern critical text miserabile (wretched). Marriott took the flattering variant. Coming one clause after 'pious cruelty' — Ferdinand expelling the Moors under the cloak of religion — the colder reading carries Machiavelli's irony, and we follow the critical text.

divergences.phrase: sine gratia, sine dignitate, praemium victoris eritis
divergences.older: you will be left, without favour or consideration, the guerdon of the conqueror
divergences.lectio: without thanks and without dignity you will be the winner's prize
divergences.note: The Roman legate's warning, which Machiavelli quotes from Livy. 'Guerdon' was antique even in 1908. The Latin is a drumbeat — sine gratia, sine dignitate — and 'prize' is exactly what praemium means: the neutral state is not a bystander to the war but the pot on the table.

divergences.phrase: pigliare el men tristo per buono
divergences.older: for choice to take the lesser evil
divergences.lectio: to take the least bad as good
divergences.note: Marriott reaches for the ready-made proverb. Machiavelli's phrase is stranger and harder: prudence is knowing that no good option exists and choosing the least bad one as if it were good. The relabeling is the point — a ruler cannot afford to keep mourning the safe course that was never on the table.

divergences.phrase: la prima coniettura che si fa del cervello d'uno signore
divergences.older: the first opinion which one forms of a prince, and of his understanding
divergences.lectio: the first guess one makes about a ruler's brains
divergences.note: Machiavelli says cervello — brain, bluntly anatomical — and coniettura, a guess made from evidence. Marriott's 'opinion of his understanding' turns a sharp field diagnostic into drawing-room talk; the chapter's whole method is reading a ruler off the men he hires.

divergences.phrase: quel primo è eccellentissimo, el secondo eccellente, el terzo inutile
divergences.older: the first is the most excellent, the second is good, the third is useless
divergences.lectio: the first is most excellent, the second excellent, the third useless
divergences.note: Marriott demotes the second class of brains to merely 'good.' Machiavelli calls it excellent — and the grade matters, because the chapter is written in consolation of second-class brains like Pandolfo's: the ruler who cannot invent can still judge, and judging is enough to keep a minister honest.

divergences.phrase: uno principe che non sia savio
divergences.older: a prince who is not inexperienced
divergences.lectio: a prince who is not wise
divergences.note: Marriott's phrase — apparently a slip for 'not experienced' — muddles the argument at its hinge. The Italian repeats the rule just laid down: it is precisely the unwise prince who can neither reconcile conflicting counsels nor see through the counselors giving them.

divergences.phrase: questa peste
divergences.older: this pest
divergences.lectio: this plague
divergences.note: Peste is pestilence, not nuisance. Courts are full of flatterers the way a city under epidemic is full of infection — self-love is the open wound it enters by, which is why Machiavelli says princes can 'barely protect themselves' from it.

divergences.phrase: li uomini sempre ti riusciranno tristi, se da una necessità non sono fatti buoni
divergences.older: men will always prove untrue to you unless they are kept honest by constraint
divergences.lectio: men will always turn out bad for you unless some necessity makes them good
divergences.note: Two restorations: tristi is 'bad' — a moral verdict wider than 'untrue' — and necessità is Machiavelli's recurring engine, the same force that makes wars just in the final chapter. Men are not held to honesty by a leash; they are made good by having no alternative.

divergences.phrase: tanto nervo che possino tenere uno esercito alla campagna
divergences.older: power enough to keep an army in the field
divergences.lectio: sinew enough to keep an army in the field
divergences.note: Nervo is sinew — the state imagined as a body with muscle in it. Marriott's 'power' flattens the anatomy, which matters in a book that keeps diagnosing states like patients: sound limbs, festering sores, a body that can still fight.

divergences.phrase: per essere quella difesa suta vile e non dependere da te
divergences.older: because that deliverance is of no avail which does not depend upon yourself
divergences.lectio: because that kind of rescue is a coward's defense and does not depend on you
divergences.note: Marriott drops the insult. Vile means base, cowardly — waiting to be called home by a disgusted populace is not merely an unreliable defense but a shameful one, and the shame is half of Machiavelli's argument against it.

divergences.phrase: la fortuna è donna, ed è necessario, volendola tenere sotto, batterla e urtarla
divergences.older: fortune is a woman, and if you wish to keep her under it is necessary to beat and ill-use her
divergences.lectio: fortune is a woman, and if you mean to keep her down you must beat her and shove her
divergences.note: The most notorious sentence in the book, kept at full force — batterla e urtarla, beat her and shove her. The brutality is the argument: audacity masters fortune, calculation courts her and loses. Softening it would falsify Machiavelli. The reader should meet the sentence as it stands and judge the writer who could write it.

divergences.phrase: uno di questi fiumi rovinosi, che, quando s'adirano
divergences.older: one of those raging rivers, which when in flood
divergences.lectio: one of those ruinous rivers that, when they grow angry
divergences.note: The river gets angry — s'adirano — and from here to the chapter's last line fortune stays a person, not a weather system. Marriott's 'in flood' makes it hydrology; the Italian makes it a temper, which is what prepares the closing figure of fortune as a woman.

divergences.phrase: meglio essere impetuoso che respettivo
divergences.older: better to be adventurous than cautious
divergences.lectio: better to be impetuous than cautious
divergences.note: Impetuoso is the chapter's technical term: it is the word for Julius II, who wins by impetuosity, and its noun impeto is the rush of the flooding river. Marriott's 'adventurous' breaks the chain that ties the pope, the river, and the audacious young men of the last sentence into one argument.

divergences.phrase: iustum enim est bellum quibus necessarium, et pia arma ubi nulla nisi in armis spes est
divergences.older: that war is just which is necessary, and arms are hallowed when there is no other hope but in them
divergences.lectio: war is just for those to whom it is necessary, and arms are holy where there is no hope left except in arms
divergences.note: At the emotional summit of the book Machiavelli quotes Livy in Latin; Marriott folds the quotation silently into his prose. We keep the epigram's balance and its claim: necessity — the engine of the whole book — is what consecrates this war.

divergences.phrase: queste illuvioni esterne
divergences.older: these foreign scourings
divergences.lectio: these foreign floods
divergences.note: Illuvione is an inundation. The barbarian invasions are the flooding river of Chapter XXV breaking over an Italy that built no dikes — Marriott's 'scourings' loses the image that binds the last two chapters into one argument.

divergences.phrase: Virtù contro al Furore / prenderà l'arme, e fia il combatter corto: / ché l'antico valore / negli italici cuor non è ancor morto
divergences.older: Virtue against fury shall advance the fight, / And it i' th' combat soon shall put to flight: / For the old Roman valour is not dead, / Nor in th' Italians' brests extinguished. (Edward Dacre, 1640)
divergences.lectio: Virtue against fury / will take up arms; and the fight will be short: / for the ancient valor / in Italian hearts is not yet dead.
divergences.note: Marriott closes with Edward Dacre's 1640 rhyming version, which pads the quatrain and adds a 'Roman' Petrarch never wrote. We render the four lines fresh and unrhymed, keeping Petrarch's short-long alternation and letting the book end where the Italian ends: on 'not yet dead.'

divergences.phrase: la liberalità, usata in modo che tu sia tenuto, ti offende
divergences.older: liberality exercised in a way that does not bring you the reputation for it, injures you (Marriott)
divergences.lectio: generosity practiced in such a way that you get the name for it does you harm
divergences.note: In the accepted text the harm attaches to showy giving: generosity used so that you are held generous — reputation-buying lavishness — is what ruins you, while quiet, genuinely virtuous giving simply goes unnoticed and earns you the name of miser anyway. Marriott's sentence points the other way and blurs the mechanism of the whole chapter: the prince is trapped because the only generosity that gets seen is the kind that bankrupts him.

divergences.phrase: col tempo sarà tenuto sempre più liberale
divergences.older: in time he will come to be more considered than if liberal (Marriott)
divergences.lectio: with time he will be thought more and more generous
divergences.note: The paradox is the point: the thrifty prince eventually earns the very name he refused to buy, because his subjects come to see that his economy is what spares their purses and pays for their defense. Marriott's 'more considered' turns a sharp irony — the miser ends up called generous — into vague esteem.

divergences.phrase: quella sua crudeltà aveva racconcia la Romagna
divergences.older: his cruelty reconciled the Romagna (Marriott)
divergences.lectio: that cruelty of his mended the Romagna
divergences.note: Racconciare is a repairman's verb — to fix something broken. Marriott's 'reconciled' makes Borgia's work sound diplomatic; Machiavelli presents the cruelty as a tool that put a broken province back in working order, and the shock of the sentence lives in that workmanlike coldness.

divergences.phrase: le amicizie che si acquistano col prezzo... si meritano, ma elle non si hanno, e a' tempi non si possano spendere
divergences.older: friendships that are obtained by payments... may indeed be earned, but they are not secured, and in time of need cannot be relied upon (Marriott)
divergences.lectio: friendships bought at a price... are paid for but not owned, and at the moment of need they cannot be spent
divergences.note: The sentence runs on a single purchase metaphor: friendships bought at a price (col prezzo) are paid for, not possessed, and cannot be 'spent' (spendere) when the need comes. Marriott closes the ledger with 'relied upon'; the Lectio keeps it open, because the cynicism is in the accounting.

divergences.phrase: né si fare paura da sé stesso
divergences.older: nor should he himself show fear (Marriott)
divergences.lectio: and should not conjure fears for himself
divergences.note: The Italian is reflexive — the prince must not manufacture his own fear, frightening himself with imagined plots into rash cruelty. It belongs with 'slow to believe and slow to act': the danger being warned against is inside his own head. Marriott's 'show fear' turns a warning about paranoia into advice about keeping up appearances.

divergences.phrase: e nelle azioni di tutti li uomini, e massime de' principi, dove non è iudizio da reclamare, si guarda al fine
divergences.older: and in the actions of all men, and especially of princes, which it is not prudent to challenge, one judges by the result (Marriott)
divergences.lectio: and in the actions of all men, and most of all of princes, where there is no court of appeal, one looks to the outcome
divergences.note: The Italian is a legal image: against another man's actions you can appeal to a judge, but above a prince there is no tribunal — so the only verdict left is the outcome. Marriott's 'not prudent to challenge' turns a structural fact about sovereign power into a piece of cautionary advice, and loses the reason appearance and result are all that count.

divergences.phrase: non partirsi dal bene, potendo, ma sapere intrare nel male, necessitato
divergences.older: not to diverge from the good if he can avoid doing so, but, if compelled, then to know how to set about it (Marriott)
divergences.lectio: not to depart from good while he can, but to know how to enter into evil when he has to
divergences.note: Machiavelli names the thing: male, evil. Marriott's 'it' lets the prince slip into an unnamed something. The force of the sentence is that 'good' stands directly against 'evil' inside a single instruction, and the translation should not blink.

divergences.phrase: colorire la inosservanzia... questa natura saperla bene colorire
divergences.older: legitimate reasons to excuse this non-observance... to disguise this characteristic (Marriott)
divergences.lectio: legitimate grounds with which to color over his breach of faith... this nature has to be painted over well
divergences.note: Colorire is a painter's verb, and Machiavelli uses it twice within a page: the broken promise and the fox's nature both get a coat of respectable color. Marriott renders it with a different word each time ('excuse,' 'disguise'); keeping one verb keeps the echo, and the image of statecraft as surface-work belongs to the chapter's argument about appearances.

divergences.phrase: da che uno principe si debbe guardare come da uno scoglio
divergences.older: from all of which a prince should guard himself as from a rock (Marriott)
divergences.lectio: a prince must guard against these as a ship guards against a reef
divergences.note: A scoglio is the sea-rock that wrecks ships, not a stone in the road; the image is of a pilot steering wide of the one thing that sinks him. Marriott's bare 'rock' loses the navigation, and with it the sense that contempt is not an embarrassment but a hull-breach.

divergences.phrase: delle quali la prima è il parlamento e la sua autorità
divergences.older: of these the first is the parliament and its authority (Marriott)
divergences.lectio: the first of these is the Parlement — the high court — and its authority
divergences.note: Machiavelli means the Parlement of Paris, a court of law, not a legislature; to a modern ear 'parliament' suggests representative government, which is precisely what the institution was not. The point of the passage is a standing tribunal that can beat down the nobility without the king's fingerprints on the stick.

divergences.phrase: uno principe, volendo mantenere lo stato, è spesso forzato a non essere buono
divergences.older: a prince wishing to keep his state is very often forced to do evil (Marriott)
divergences.lectio: a prince who wants to hold his state is often forced not to be good
divergences.note: The Italian repeats, word for word, the thesis of Chapter XV — the prince must learn how not to be good (essere non buono). Marriott's 'forced to do evil' breaks the deliberate echo and overstates the claim: Machiavelli's phrase is a negation of goodness, colder and more careful than a positive command to do evil.

divergences.phrase: uno stato nuovo, che come membro si aggiunga al suo vecchio
divergences.older: a new state, which he adds as a province to his old one (Marriott)
divergences.lectio: a new state that is joined like a limb to his old one
divergences.note: Membro is a body part: the new state is grafted onto the body of the old. That is why the treatment that follows reads like surgery — strip its arms, soften its fighting men — the limb is to be made incapable of moving on its own. Marriott's 'province' is administrative where the Italian is anatomical.

divergences.phrase: alcuni hanno nutrito inimicizie contro a sé medesimi... nutrirsi con astuzia qualche inimicizia
divergences.older: others have fostered enmities against themselves... ought with craft to foster some animosity against himself (Marriott)
divergences.lectio: some have fed enmities against themselves... should cunningly feed some enmity against himself
divergences.note: Nutrire is to feed a living thing. The prince keeps a tame hostility alive on purpose — husbanded like an animal, so it can be slaughtered for show when the moment serves. 'Foster' is close, but 'feed' keeps the deliberateness of the husbandry, and the same verb returns when the Venetians nurse the factions in their cities.

divergences.phrase: ha fatto e farà più guerra alla casa Sforza
divergences.older: has made, and will make, more trouble for the house of Sforza than any other disorder in the state (Marriott)
divergences.lectio: has made and will make more wars against the house of Sforza
divergences.note: Machiavelli says guerra: the citadel does not inconvenience the dynasty, it fights it — a standing provocation that puts the ruling house and its own city permanently under arms against each other. Marriott's 'trouble' mislays the force of the claim, which is that a fortress can be an enemy you built yourself.

segments.text: All states, all dominions that have held and hold power over men, have been and are either republics or principalities.
Principalities are either hereditary, where one bloodline has ruled for a long time, or they are new.

The new ones are either new outright, as Milan was to Francesco Sforza, or they are like limbs grafted onto the hereditary state of the prince who acquires them, as the kingdom of Naples is to the King of Spain.

Dominions acquired this way are accustomed either to living under a prince or to being free; and they are acquired either with the arms of others or with one's own, either by fortune or by virtù — a man's own skill and nerve.

I will leave republics aside, since I have discussed them at length elsewhere. I will turn only to principalities, taking up the threads laid out above, and ask how these principalities can be governed and kept.

I say at once that hereditary states, accustomed to the bloodline of their prince, are far less difficult to hold than new ones. It is enough not to break the customs of one's ancestors, and to play for time when events turn; then a prince of ordinary industry will always keep his state, unless some extraordinary and overwhelming force strips him of it — and even stripped of it, he wins it back the moment the usurper stumbles.

Italy gives us an example in the Duke of Ferrara, who held out against the assaults of the Venetians in '84, and of Pope Julius in '10, for no other reason than that his house was old in that dominion. For the hereditary prince has fewer reasons to give offense, and less need to; hence he is more loved; and unless outrageous vices make him hated, it stands to reason that his own people are naturally well disposed toward him. In the age and continuity of his rule, the memories of innovation and the causes of it are extinguished — for one change always leaves jutting brickwork for the next to build on.

But in the new principality the difficulties begin. First, if it is not new through and through but a limb joined to a larger state (call the whole thing, taken together, a mixed principality), its instability springs first of all from a natural difficulty found in every new principality: men change masters willingly, believing they will be better off, and that belief puts arms in their hands against the man who rules them. In this they are deceived, for experience soon teaches them that they are worse off. And that follows from another necessity, natural and ordinary: a new prince is always forced to injure the very people he acquires, both with his soldiers and with the countless other abuses a new conquest drags behind it.

So you have for enemies everyone you injured in seizing the principality, and you cannot keep as friends the men who put you there, since you cannot satisfy them as they had expected — and you cannot use strong medicine against them either, being in their debt. For however strong your armies, you always need the goodwill of the locals to enter a province.

For these reasons Louis the Twelfth, King of France, took Milan quickly and lost it quickly; and to take it from him the first time, Lodovico's own forces were enough. For the people who had opened the gates to him, finding themselves cheated of the future they had promised themselves, could not stomach the abuses of the new prince. It is quite true that when rebel territory is taken a second time it is not lost so easily, for the prince, with fewer scruples now, uses the rebellion as his license to punish the guilty, expose the suspects, and reinforce himself wherever he is weakest. So the first time, to make France lose Milan, it was enough for Duke Lodovico to raise a revolt on the borders; to make her lose it the second time took the whole world combined against her, her armies destroyed and driven out of Italy — and that came about for the reasons given above.

Nevertheless, Milan was taken from France both the first time and the second. The general reasons for the first have been given; it remains to give the reasons for the second, and to see what remedies Louis had — what remedies anyone in his place would have — to hold a new acquisition more firmly than the King of France held his.

Now I say that the dominions a conqueror gains and joins to an older state of his own either belong to the same country and language, or they do not. When they do, holding them is very easy, especially when they are not used to living free; to possess them securely, it is enough to have extinguished the line of the prince who ruled them. For the rest, leave the old conditions alone; where customs match, men live quietly together — as they have in Brittany, Burgundy, Gascony, and Normandy, so long bound to France. There may be some difference of language, but the customs are alike, and people manage easily among themselves. Whoever acquires such lands and means to keep them must see to just two things: that the old prince's bloodline is extinguished, and that neither laws nor taxes are altered. In a very short time the new territory and the old principality become one body.

But when states are acquired in a province that differs in language, in customs, and in institutions, here the difficulties begin, and here you need great fortune and great industry to keep hold. One of the best and most immediate remedies is for the conqueror to go and live there in person. That makes the possession more secure and more lasting — as it has for the Turk in Greece, who, with every other measure he took for holding that state, could not have kept it without settling in it. On the spot, you see disorders as they are born, and you can put them down at once; from a distance, you hear of them only when they are full grown, and past curing. Besides this, the province is not stripped bare by your officials; the subjects are satisfied by quick access to their prince, which gives them more cause to love him if they mean to be good, and more cause to fear him if they do not. Any foreign power thinking of attacking the state hesitates; a prince who lives in it is dispossessed only with the greatest difficulty.

The other and better remedy is to plant colonies in one or two places that will serve as shackles on that state; either you do this, or you must keep large numbers of cavalry and infantry there instead. Colonies cost little. At little or no expense of his own, the prince sends them out and keeps them there, and he injures only those he strips of fields and houses to give to the new settlers — a minority of that state, and one left poor and scattered, which can never do him harm. All the rest remain uninjured on one side, and therefore easily quieted, and frightened on the other, in case what happened to the despoiled should happen next to them. I conclude: colonies cost nothing, are more loyal, and give less offense; and the offended, poor and scattered, cannot hurt you, as I have said. For here is a thing to note: men should be either treated well or snuffed out. They can avenge a light injury; a fatal one they cannot. So the injury done to a man must be of the kind that leaves no revenge to fear.

But keep armed men there instead of colonies and the cost multiplies: the whole revenue of the state goes to feed its garrison, until the acquisition runs at a loss. And it gives far more offense, since the whole state feels the injury as the garrison shifts its quarters from place to place. Everyone tastes the hardship; everyone becomes an enemy — and they are enemies who can still hurt you, beaten but still at home. On every count, then, a garrison is as useless as a colony is useful.

Again, a prince holding a province unlike his own, as I have said, should make himself the head and protector of the smaller powers around him, work to weaken the strong ones, and take care that no foreigner as powerful as himself finds a way in by any accident. For such a one will always be called in by the discontented, out of too much ambition or out of fear — as the Ætolians once brought the Romans into Greece; indeed, into every province the Romans entered, they were brought by its own inhabitants. And the order of things is this: the moment a powerful foreigner enters a province, all its lesser powers attach themselves to him, driven by envy of the power that has stood over them — so that as regards these lesser powers he need not lift a finger to win them, since all together they immediately and willingly make one mass with the state he has taken there. He has only to see that they do not lay hands on too much strength and too much authority; then, with his own forces and their goodwill, he can easily bring down the powerful and remain, in everything, the arbiter of that province. And whoever fails to manage this part well will quickly lose what he has gained — and while he holds it, will find in it infinite difficulties and vexations.

In the provinces they seized, the Romans kept these rules exactly: they planted colonies; they humored the lesser powers without increasing their strength; they beat down the strong; and they never let a powerful foreigner win credit there. The province of Greece will do as the one example. The Romans kept the Achaeans and the Ætolians as friends; the kingdom of Macedonia was humbled; Antiochus was driven out. Yet no merit of the Achaeans or the Ætolians ever bought them leave to enlarge a state of theirs; no persuasion from Philip ever induced the Romans to be his friends until they had brought him low; and all the power of Antiochus never made them consent to his keeping any state in that province. For the Romans did in these cases what every wise prince must do: attend not only to present disorders but to future ones, and ward those off with every kind of effort. Seen from far off, they are easily remedied; wait until they are on top of you, and the medicine is too late — the disease has become incurable. It is as the physicians say of the wasting fever: early on, it is easy to cure and hard to detect; with time, neither detected nor treated, it becomes easy to detect and impossible to cure. So it goes in matters of state. Recognize evils while they are still forming — a gift given only to the prudent — and they are cured quickly. Fail to recognize them, let them grow until anyone can see them, and no remedy remains. So the Romans, seeing troubles while they were still distant, always dealt with them then, and never let one run on merely to escape a war; they knew that a war is not escaped — only postponed, to the advantage of others. So they chose to fight Philip and Antiochus in Greece rather than have to fight them in Italy. They could, at the time, have avoided both. They chose not to. And they never cared for the saying that is forever in the mouths of the wise men of our day — enjoy the benefit of time. They preferred the benefit of their own virtù and prudence. For time drives everything before it, and can bring good as easily as evil, evil as easily as good.

But let us return to France and consider whether she did any of the things I have named. I will speak of Louis and not of Charles, since Louis held possessions in Italy longer, and his course is the easier to read; and you will see that he did the contrary of everything that must be done to hold a state unlike one's own.

King Louis was brought into Italy by the ambition of the Venetians, who meant his coming to win them half the state of Lombardy. I will not blame the king for the part he took: wanting a first foothold in Italy, and having no friends in the province — every door barred to him, indeed, by the conduct of Charles — he had to take whatever friendships he could get; and the plan would have succeeded quickly enough had he made no errors elsewhere. With Lombardy taken, the king at once won back the standing Charles had thrown away: Genoa yielded; the Florentines became his friends; the Marquess of Mantua, the Duke of Ferrara, the Bentivogli, my lady of Forli, the lords of Faenza, of Pesaro, of Rimini, of Camerino, of Piombino, the Lucchese, the Pisans, the Sienese — all came forward to offer him their friendship. Then the Venetians had leisure to consider the rashness of what they had done: to gain themselves two towns in Lombardy, they had made the king master of two-thirds of Italy.

Consider now how little trouble the king would have had in holding his standing in Italy if he had observed the rules set down above and kept all those friends of his secure and defended. They were many, they were weak, they were afraid — some of the Church, some of the Venetians — and so they were bound always to stand with him; and through them he could easily have secured himself against the powers that remained great. But he was no sooner in Milan than he did the reverse, lending Pope Alexander a hand to seize the Romagna. And it did not occur to him that with this decision he was weakening himself — casting off his friends, and the people who had thrown themselves into his lap — while making the Church great, stacking so much temporal power onto the spiritual power that already gives it such authority. Having made the first error, he was dragged into the rest, until finally, to check Alexander's ambition and keep him from becoming master of Tuscany, he was forced to come into Italy himself.

And as if it were not enough to have made the Church great and stripped himself of his friends, he then wanted the kingdom of Naples — and divided it with the King of Spain. Where he had been sole arbiter of Italy he installed a partner, so that the ambitious men of that province, and the malcontents of his own party, would have somewhere to turn; and where he could have left in that kingdom a king who was his pensioner, dependent on him, he removed him — and put in his place a man capable of driving out Louis himself.

The wish to acquire is a thing truly natural and ordinary; when men who can, acquire, they will be praised for it, or at least not blamed. The error, and the blame, come when men who cannot are set on acquiring anyway. If France could have taken Naples with her own forces, she should have taken it; since she could not, she should not have split it. The split she made of Lombardy with the Venetians had an excuse: it bought her entry into Italy. This one had no such necessity behind it, and so it stands condemned.

Louis, then, had made five errors: he destroyed the lesser powers; he increased the power of one already great in Italy; he brought into Italy a foreign power of the first rank; he did not come to live there; he did not plant colonies. And even these five, in his lifetime, might not have hurt him had he not made a sixth: taking their dominions from the Venetians. Had he never made the Church great, never brought Spain into Italy, then cutting the Venetians down would have been reasonable, even necessary. But having taken those first steps, he should never have consented to their ruin: while the Venetians were strong, they would have kept everyone else clear of any venture against Lombardy — partly because the Venetians would allow no such venture unless it ended with Lombardy theirs, partly because the others had no wish to take it from France only to hand it to the Venetians, and no nerve to take on both together.

And if anyone says that King Louis ceded the Romagna to Alexander, and the kingdom to Spain, to avoid a war — I answer with the reasons given above: a disorder should never be allowed to run on for the sake of avoiding a war, because the war is not avoided; it is deferred, to your own disadvantage. And if others cite the pledge the king had given the Pope — this campaign in exchange for the dissolution of his marriage and a cardinal's hat for Rouen — I answer with what I will say further on about the word of princes, and how far it should be kept.

So King Louis lost Lombardy by keeping none of the conditions kept by others who have taken provinces and meant to hold them. Nor is there any miracle in this — it is ordinary, and entirely reasonable. I said as much at Nantes to the Cardinal of Rouen, when Valentino — as Cesare Borgia, Pope Alexander's son, was commonly called — was occupying the Romagna. When the Cardinal of Rouen told me that the Italians understood nothing of war, I answered that the French understood nothing of statecraft; for if they did, they would not be letting the Church grow so great. And experience has borne it out: the greatness of the Church and of Spain in Italy was made by France, and France's ruin was made by them. From which a general rule can be drawn that never fails, or rarely: whoever makes another man powerful ruins himself. He builds that power with either cunning or force — and cunning and force are exactly what the man he raised will never trust.

sections.label: Chapter IV
sections.title: Why Darius's Kingdom Did Not Rebel

segments.text: Considering how hard it is to hold a newly acquired state, one might wonder at this: Alexander the Great made himself master of Asia in a few years and died when he had barely settled it — the very moment, it would seem, for the whole empire to rebel. Yet Alexander's successors held it, and the only difficulty they had in keeping it was the one their own ambition bred among themselves.

I answer that all the principalities on record have been governed in one of two ways: either by one prince, with everyone else his servant, some of them helping him govern the kingdom as ministers, by his grace and license; or by a prince and by barons, who hold their rank not by their master's favor but by ancient blood. Such barons have states and subjects of their own — subjects who recognize them as lords and bear them a natural affection. In states governed by a prince and his servants, the prince stands higher in men's eyes, for in the whole province no one is acknowledged superior but him; if people obey anyone else, they obey a minister and an official, and feel no particular love for him.

The living examples of these two kinds of government are the Turk and the King of France. The whole monarchy of the Turk is governed by one lord; the rest are his servants. He divides his kingdom into sanjaks, sends out administrators, and moves and replaces them as he pleases. The King of France, by contrast, sits in the midst of an ancient multitude of lords, each acknowledged and loved by subjects of his own; they have their privileges, and the king cannot touch them without danger to himself. Consider these two states, then, and you will find the difficulty is in conquering the Turk's — but once conquered, it is held with great ease. The reasons his kingdom is hard to seize are these: an invader cannot be called in by the princes of the realm, and cannot hope for a revolt in the ruler's own circle to ease his enterprise. That follows from what was said above: the ruler's ministers, being all slaves, and bound men, are corrupted only with great effort, and even corrupted they are worth little, since they cannot pull the people after them, for the reasons given. So whoever attacks the Turk must expect to find him united, and had better count on his own strength rather than on the other side's disorders. But once the Turk is beaten — broken in the field past raising new armies — there is nothing left to fear but the prince's bloodline. Extinguish that, and no one remains to be feared, for none of the others has any credit with the people; and just as the conqueror could expect nothing from them before his victory, he need fear nothing from them after it.

The opposite holds in kingdoms governed like France. There you can enter with ease by winning over some baron of the realm, for malcontents are always to be found, and men who want things changed. Such men, for the reasons given, can open the road into the state and hand you the victory. But keeping it afterward brings infinite trouble, from those who helped you and from those you crushed alike. Nor is it enough to have extinguished the prince's line, because the lords remain, ready to make themselves heads of new movements; and being able neither to satisfy them nor to snuff them out, you lose the state the first time the occasion offers.

Now consider what kind of government Darius had, and you will find it like the kingdom of the Turk. So Alexander had first to smash him in the field and sweep him from open country; and after that victory, with Darius dead, the state stayed securely in Alexander's hands, for the reasons argued above. Had his successors stayed united, they could have enjoyed it at their leisure — no tumults arose in that kingdom but the ones they raised themselves.

But states ordered like France cannot be possessed so quietly. Hence the repeated rebellions of Spain, of France, and of Greece against the Romans — all because of the many principalities those provinces contained. As long as the memory of them lasted, Rome's hold was never sure; when that memory was extinguished by the power and long duration of the empire, the hold became secure. And later, when the Romans fought among themselves, each commander could carry with him the part of those provinces where his own authority had taken root; the bloodlines of the old lords being extinguished, the provinces acknowledged no one but Romans.

Keep all this in mind, and no one will wonder at the ease with which Alexander kept his hold on the empire of Asia, or at the trouble others — Pyrrhus among many — have had in keeping what they won. It comes not from the little or great virtù of the conqueror, but from the difference in what was conquered.

When states acquired in the way I have described are accustomed to living free under their own laws, there are three ways to hold them: the first is to ruin them; the second is to go and live there in person; the third is to let them live on under their own laws, taking a tribute from them and setting up inside a government of a few men who will keep the state friendly to you. For such a government, being the prince's creature, knows it cannot stand without his friendship and his power, and will do everything to keep him standing. And a city used to living free, if you mean to preserve it at all, is held more easily through its own citizens than by any other means.

Take the Spartans and the Romans. The Spartans held Athens and Thebes by setting up governments of a few men in them; they lost them anyway. The Romans, to hold Capua, Carthage, and Numantia, demolished them, and did not lose them. They tried to hold Greece more or less as the Spartans had held it — leaving it free, leaving it its laws — and it failed; to keep the province they were forced to demolish many of its cities. For the truth is that there is no secure way to possess such cities except to ruin them. And whoever becomes master of a city accustomed to living free, and does not destroy it, should expect to be destroyed by it; for in rebellion it will always find its rallying cry in the name of liberty and in its own old order, which neither the length of years nor any amount of good treatment ever makes it forget. Do what you like, provide what you like: unless the inhabitants are split apart or scattered, they never forget that name or that order, and at every accident they run straight back to both — as Pisa did after a hundred years in bondage to the Florentines.

But when cities or provinces are used to living under a prince and his bloodline is extinguished, then — trained to obey, their old prince gone — they can neither agree on a new prince from among themselves nor manage to live free. They are slower to take up arms, and a prince can win them more easily and hold them more securely. In republics there is more life, more hatred, more appetite for revenge. The memory of their old liberty gives them no rest — it cannot. So the safest way is to snuff them out — or to go and live there.

sections.label: Chapter VI
sections.title: By Your Own Arms and Virtù

segments.text: No one should be surprised if, in speaking of principalities entirely new, I bring in the greatest examples of prince and of state. Men almost always walk in paths beaten by others, and conduct their affairs by imitation; but the paths of others cannot be followed exactly, and you cannot reach the virtù of the man you imitate. So a prudent man should always enter by paths beaten by great men, and imitate those who have been most excellent — so that if his own virtù does not reach theirs, at least it carries some scent of it. He should do as the clever archers do when the target looks too far off: knowing how far their bow will carry, they aim well above the mark — not to drive the arrow to that height, but to hit, by so high an aim, the mark they intend.

I say, then, that in principalities entirely new, where there is a new prince, holding on is more or less difficult according to the virtù of the man who acquires them. And since becoming prince from private citizen presupposes either virtù or fortune, one or the other of these, it seems, must ease many of the difficulties. Even so, the man who has leaned less on fortune has held on longer. It also helps when the prince, having no other state, is forced to come and live in this one in person.

But to come to those who became princes by their own virtù and not by fortune: the most excellent, I say, are Moses, Cyrus, Romulus, Theseus, and their like. And though Moses should hardly be discussed, being a mere executor of things ordered by God, still he deserves admiration, if only for the grace that made him worthy to speak with God. But consider Cyrus and the others who acquired or founded kingdoms: you will find them all admirable; and if you weigh their particular actions and arrangements, they will not look much different from those of Moses, who had so great a teacher. Examine their actions and their lives, and you will find they owed nothing to fortune but opportunity — the raw material they shaped into whatever form seemed best to them. Without that opportunity the virtù of their minds would have gone out; without that virtù, the opportunity would have come in vain.

It was necessary, then, that Moses find the people of Israel in Egypt, enslaved and ground down by the Egyptians, so that to escape their servitude they would be ready to follow him. It was necessary that Romulus not stay in Alba, and that he be exposed at birth, if he was to become King of Rome and founder of that fatherland. It was necessary that Cyrus find the Persians sick of the empire of the Medes, and the Medes gone soft from long peace. Theseus could not have shown his virtù had he not found the Athenians scattered. These opportunities made these men fortunate, then, and their surpassing virtù made them recognize the opportunity; and by it their countries were ennobled and made supremely happy.

Men like these, who become princes by paths of virtù, acquire their principality with difficulty but hold it with ease. The difficulties in acquiring come partly from the new orders and methods they are forced to introduce to found their state and secure it. And it should be kept in mind that nothing is harder to take in hand, more doubtful of success, or more dangerous to manage than making yourself the leader in introducing a new order of things. The innovator has enemies in everyone who did well under the old order, and lukewarm defenders in everyone who might do well under the new. The lukewarmness comes partly from fear of the opponents, who have the laws on their side, and partly from the incredulity of men — who never truly believe in anything new until solid experience has shown it to them. So whenever the enemies of the new order get their chance to attack, they attack like partisans, and the others defend half-heartedly; and between them the prince is put at risk.

If we want to examine this part thoroughly, we must ask whether these innovators stand on their own or depend on others — that is, whether they must beg to carry their work through, or whether they can force it. When they must beg, they always end badly and accomplish nothing. But when they depend on their own strength and can use force, they are rarely in danger. This is why all armed prophets have conquered, and the unarmed have been destroyed. For besides everything said already, the nature of peoples is fickle: it is easy to persuade them of a thing, and hard to hold them to the persuasion. So matters must be ordered in such a way that when they no longer believe, they can be made to believe by force.

Moses, Cyrus, Theseus, and Romulus could not have made their orders obeyed for long had they been unarmed — as happened in our own time to Fra Girolamo Savonarola, who was ruined along with his new order the moment the crowd began not to believe him; and he had no way to hold firm the ones who had believed, or to make the unbelievers believe. Men like these, then, face great difficulty in carrying the work through: all their dangers lie on the way up, and virtù must get them past. But once they are past — once they are held in reverence, and have wiped out the men who envied them their standing — they remain powerful, secure, honored, and happy.

To such lofty examples I want to add a lesser one; but it keeps some proportion with them, and I mean it to stand for every other case of its kind: Hiero the Syracusan. From private citizen, he became Prince of Syracuse — and he owed nothing to fortune but opportunity. The Syracusans, being oppressed, elected him their captain; from there he earned his promotion to prince. And he was of such virtù even in private life that the man who wrote of him said he lacked nothing of a king but the kingdom. He abolished the old militia and raised a new one; he dropped the old friendships and made new ones; and once the friendships and the soldiers were his own, he could build any building on that foundation — so that what cost him great effort to acquire cost him little to keep.

Those who rise from private citizen to prince by fortune alone rise with little effort but hold on with a great deal. They have no trouble on the way up, because they fly there; all the trouble begins once they land. Such are the men who are handed a state, either for money or as a favor from whoever grants it — as happened to many in Greece, in the cities of Ionia and the Hellespont, where Darius made princes so they would hold the cities for his security and his glory; and as happened to those emperors who rose from private citizens to the throne by bribing the soldiers. Men like this stand simply on the goodwill and the fortune of whoever raised them — two utterly fickle and unstable things — and they neither know how to hold the position nor can they. They do not know how, because unless a man has great intelligence and virtù, it is not reasonable that he should know how to command after a lifetime as a private citizen; and they cannot, because they have no forces of their own that they can count on to be loyal and faithful.

Besides, states that spring up overnight, like everything else in nature that is born and grows too fast, cannot have put down roots and connections deep enough to survive the first storm — unless, as I said, the men who become princes overnight have so much virtù that they know at once how to hold what fortune has dropped in their laps, and can lay afterward the foundations that others lay before they become princes.

For these two ways of becoming prince — by virtù or by fortune — I want to offer two examples from within living memory: Francesco Sforza and Cesare Borgia. Francesco, by the right means and by great virtù of his own, rose from private citizen to Duke of Milan, and what he had acquired with a thousand pains he kept with little effort. Cesare Borgia, on the other hand — called Duke Valentino by the people — acquired his state by his father's fortune and lost it the same way, even though he did everything and used every means a prudent and capable man should use to sink his roots into the states that the arms and fortune of others had given him.

Because, as was said above, whoever does not lay his foundations in advance might, with great virtù, lay them later — though it costs the architect trouble and puts the building at risk. If you consider all the steps the duke took, you will see that he laid great foundations for his future power; and I do not think it beside the point to go through them, because I would not know what better lessons to give a new prince than the example of his actions. And if his arrangements came to nothing in the end, it was not his fault: it was an extraordinary and extreme malice of fortune.

Alexander the Sixth, wanting to make his son the duke great, faced plenty of difficulties, present and future. First, he saw no way to make him master of any state that was not a state of the Church; and he knew that if he moved to take from the Church, the Duke of Milan and the Venetians would not stand for it — Faenza and Rimini were already under Venetian protection. Beyond that, he saw the arms of Italy, especially the ones he might have used, in the hands of men with every reason to fear a greater Pope — the Orsini, the Colonnesi, and their followers. It was necessary, then, to upset this arrangement and throw their states into disorder, so as to make himself securely master of part of them. That proved easy, because he found the Venetians, for reasons of their own, already working to bring the French back into Italy; he not only did not oppose it, he smoothed the way by annulling King Louis's old marriage. So the king came into Italy with the help of the Venetians and the consent of Alexander; and no sooner was he in Milan than the Pope had troops from him for the campaign in the Romagna, which was surrendered to him on the king's reputation. Having taken the Romagna, then, and beaten the Colonnesi, the duke wanted to hold what he had and push further, but two things stood in his way: his own forces, which did not look loyal to him, and the will of France. He feared that the Orsini arms he had been using would fail under him — that they would not only block further gains but take from him what he had already gained — and that the king would do the same. He got his proof about the Orsini when, after taking Faenza, he attacked Bologna and watched them go cold on the assault; and he learned the king's mind when, after seizing the Duchy of Urbino, he moved on Tuscany and the king made him back off. At that point the duke resolved to depend no longer on the arms and fortune of others.

His first move was to weaken the Orsini and Colonna factions in Rome. He won over all their gentlemen adherents by making them his own gentlemen — paying them well and honoring them, according to their rank, with commands and offices — so that within a few months their old party loyalties died out and the whole allegiance turned to the duke. After that, having already scattered the men of the Colonna house, he waited for his chance to crush the Orsini, and when it came he used it well. The Orsini, realizing too late that the greatness of the duke and the Church meant their ruin, called a meeting at Magione, in Perugian territory. Out of that came the revolt of Urbino, the uprisings in the Romagna, and endless dangers for the duke — all of which he overcame with the help of the French. Then, his reputation restored, and trusting neither France nor any other outside force enough to put them to the test, he turned to deception. And he knew so well how to disguise his mind that the Orsini themselves — through Signor Pagolo, whom the duke took care to reassure with every courtesy, giving him money, clothes, and horses — were reconciled to him; and their simplicity delivered them into his hands at Sinigalia. So with the leaders wiped out and their partisans turned into his friends, the duke had laid quite good foundations for his power: he held all the Romagna along with the Duchy of Urbino, and above all he had won the Romagna itself, whose people had begun to taste prosperity under him. And because this part deserves notice, and imitation by others, I do not want to pass over it.

When the duke took the Romagna, he found it had been run by weak lords, quicker to strip their subjects than to govern them, who had given the province more cause for division than for unity, so that it was rife with theft, feuds, and every sort of outrage. He judged that to make it peaceful and obedient to the ruler's arm, it needed good government; so he set over it Messer Ramiro d'Orco, a cruel and efficient man, and gave him the fullest power. In a short time Ramiro made the province peaceful and united, and won an enormous reputation doing it. Then the duke judged that such excessive authority was no longer wanted, fearing it would breed hatred; and he set up a civil court in the middle of the province, under an excellent president, where every city had its advocate. And because he knew the past severities had bred some hatred against himself, he wanted to purge the minds of the people and win them over completely — to show that whatever cruelty had been done had come not from him but from the harsh nature of his minister. So, having found his moment, one morning at Cesena he had Ramiro laid out in two pieces on the piazza, with a block of wood and a bloody knife beside him. The ferocity of that spectacle left the people at once satisfied and stunned.

But let us return to where we left off. I say that the duke now found himself powerful enough, and partly insured against present dangers — armed his own way, and having largely destroyed the neighboring forces that could hurt him — and what remained, if he meant to go on conquering, was France; because he knew the king, who had seen his mistake too late, would not tolerate it. So he began to look for new alliances and to stall France over the expedition she was making toward the kingdom of Naples, against the Spaniards besieging Gaeta. His intention was to secure himself against them, and he would soon have managed it if Alexander had lived.

That was how he handled things present. As for things to come, he had to fear, first, that a new head of the Church would be no friend to him and would try to take back what Alexander had given him. He thought to secure himself against that in four ways. First, by wiping out the bloodlines of the lords he had despoiled, to strip the Pope of that pretext. Second, by winning over all the gentlemen of Rome, as I have said, so as to hold the Pope in check through them. Third, by making the College of Cardinals his, as far as he could. Fourth, by acquiring so much power before the Pope died that he could withstand a first attack on his own. Of these four things, by the time Alexander died, he had accomplished three. Of the despoiled lords he had killed as many as he could reach, and very few escaped; the Roman gentlemen were won; and in the College he had the largest party. As for new acquisitions, he had designs on Tuscany; he already possessed Perugia and Piombino, and had taken Pisa under his protection. And since he no longer had to defer to France — the French had already been stripped of the kingdom of Naples by the Spaniards, so that each side now had to buy his friendship — he pounced on Pisa. After that, Lucca and Siena would fold at once, partly out of spite toward the Florentines and partly out of fear; and the Florentines would have had no remedy. Had he brought this off — and he was bringing it off the very year Alexander died — he would have gathered such force and such reputation that he would have stood on his own, no longer depending on the fortune and forces of another, but on his own power and virtù.

But Alexander died five years after the duke first drew his sword. He left him with only the state of Romagna consolidated, everything else in the air, caught between two very powerful enemy armies, and deathly ill. Yet there was such ferocity and such virtù in the duke — he understood so well how men are won or lost, and the foundations he had laid in so short a time were so sound — that if he had not had those armies on his back, or if he had been healthy, he would have ridden out every difficulty. And that his foundations were good, you could see: the Romagna waited for him more than a month; in Rome, half dead, he was safe; and though the Baglioni, the Vitelli, and the Orsini came to Rome, they could raise nothing against him. If he could not make Pope the man he wanted, he could at least keep out the man he did not want. Had he been healthy when Alexander died, everything would have gone easily for him. He told me himself, on the day Julius the Second was elected, that he had thought through everything that could happen when his father died, and had found a remedy for all of it — except that he never imagined that when the day came, he too would be at the point of death.

Gathering up all the duke's actions, then, I would not know how to fault him. On the contrary, it seems right to hold him up, as I have done, as a model for all those who rise to rule by fortune and the arms of others. With his great spirit and his high aims, he could not have conducted himself otherwise; only the shortness of Alexander's life and his own sickness stood against his designs. So whoever judges it necessary, in a new principality, to secure himself against enemies; to win friends; to conquer by force or by fraud; to make himself loved and feared by the people, followed and respected by the soldiers; to wipe out those who can or must hurt him; to replace the old order with new; to be severe and gracious, magnanimous and open-handed; to destroy a disloyal army and build a new one; to keep the friendship of kings and princes on such terms that they help him gladly and cross him carefully — such a man can find no fresher example than this man's actions.

The one thing he can be blamed for is the election of Julius as Pope: there he chose badly. Because, as I said, if he could not make a Pope of his own, he could keep the papacy from anyone he chose — and he should never have consented to the elevation of any cardinal he had injured, or any who, once Pope, would have reason to fear him. For men do injury out of fear or out of hatred. Those he had injured included San Pietro ad Vincula, Colonna, San Giorgio, and Ascanio; all the rest, on becoming Pope, would have had cause to fear him — except Rouen and the Spaniards: the Spaniards through kinship and obligation, Rouen through power, having the kingdom of France behind him. So the duke's first choice should have been a Spanish Pope; failing that, he should have consented to Rouen, not San Pietro ad Vincula. Whoever believes that with great men new favors erase old injuries is deceiving himself. The duke erred in this election, and it was the cause of his final ruin.

But since there are two more ways a private citizen can become a prince, neither of which can be put down entirely to fortune or to virtù, I cannot leave them out — though one of them could be treated at more length where republics are discussed. These are: when a man rises to the principality by some criminal and wicked path, and when a private citizen becomes prince of his native city by the favor of his fellow citizens. Speaking of the first way, I will show it by two examples, one ancient and one recent, without otherwise weighing the merits of this course — because for anyone who needs it, I judge these two are enough to imitate.

Agathocles the Sicilian became King of Syracuse not merely from private life but from the bottom — from a low and abject start. The son of a potter, he lived a criminal life at every stage of his career. Yet he joined his crimes to such virtù of mind and body that, after entering the militia, he rose through its ranks to be Praetor of Syracuse. Once settled in that rank, he decided to become prince — to hold by violence, and owing nothing to anyone, what had been granted him by consent.
