He reached an understanding about his plan with Amilcar the Carthaginian, who was campaigning with his armies in Sicily; then one morning he assembled the people and the senate of Syracuse as if he had business of the Republic to discuss, and at a prearranged signal his soldiers killed all the senators and the richest of the people. With them dead, he seized and held the rule of that city without any civil strife. And though the Carthaginians twice defeated him and finally besieged him, he not only defended his city: leaving part of his forces to hold off the siege, he attacked Africa with the rest, lifted the siege of Syracuse in short order, and drove the Carthaginians to such extremity that they were forced to come to terms with him — to content themselves with Africa and leave Sicily to Agathocles.

Whoever weighs this man's actions and virtù, then, will find little or nothing that can be credited to fortune. As I said, he came to the principality not by anyone's favor but up through the ranks of the militia, earning every step with a thousand hardships and dangers, and afterward held his place by many bold and risky decisions. And yet it cannot be called virtù to kill your fellow citizens, betray your friends, and be without faith, without pity, without religion. Such methods can win empire, but not glory. If you consider Agathocles' virtù in walking into dangers and walking out of them, and his greatness of spirit in bearing and beating adversity, there is no reason to rank him below the most celebrated captains. All the same, his savage cruelty and inhumanity, and his countless crimes, do not allow him to be honored among the truly excellent men. So what he achieved cannot be credited to fortune — and it cannot be credited to virtù.

In our own times, under Alexander the Sixth, there is Oliverotto da Fermo. Left fatherless years before as a small child, he was raised by a maternal uncle, Giovanni Fogliani, and in his early youth sent to soldier under Pagolo Vitelli, so that a training in that discipline might carry him to some high rank in the profession. After Pagolo died he served under his brother Vitellozzo, and in a very short time — being clever, and vigorous in body and mind — he became the first man of his company. But it seemed servile to him to take orders from others, so he resolved to seize Fermo — with the help of certain citizens of Fermo who preferred their city enslaved to their city free, and with the backing of the Vitelleschi. He wrote to Giovanni Fogliani that after so many years away he wanted to come see him and his city, and to have some look at his own inheritance; and since he had labored for nothing but honor, he wished to arrive honorably, escorted by a hundred horsemen of his friends and servants, so that his fellow citizens would see he had not spent his years for nothing; and he begged Giovanni to arrange an honorable reception from the people of Fermo — which would do honor not only to him but to Giovanni himself, who had raised him.

Giovanni failed in no courtesy owed his nephew. He had him honorably received by the Fermians and lodged him in his own house — where Oliverotto, after a few days spent quietly arranging what his coming crime required, gave a formal banquet and invited Giovanni Fogliani and all the leading men of Fermo. When the food and the usual entertainments of such banquets were done, Oliverotto artfully steered the talk to weighty matters — the greatness of Pope Alexander and his son Cesare, and their undertakings. Giovanni and the others were answering when he rose all at once, saying these were things to discuss in a more private room, and withdrew to a chamber; Giovanni and all the other citizens followed him in. No sooner were they seated than soldiers came out of hiding and killed Giovanni and all the rest. After the slaughter, Oliverotto mounted his horse, rode the town, and besieged the chief magistracy in its palace; so that out of fear the people obeyed him and formed a government, of which he made himself prince. And with everyone dead who, being discontented, could have hurt him, he strengthened himself with new civil and military ordinances — so that within the year he held the principality, he was not only secure inside the city of Fermo but feared by all its neighbors. Rooting him out would have been as hard as rooting out Agathocles, had he not let himself be tricked by Cesare Borgia, when at Sinigalia, as was told above, the duke took the Orsini and the Vitelli and took him with them. There, one year after the parricide he had committed, he was strangled, together with Vitellozzo, who had been his teacher in virtù and in crime.

Some may wonder how it could happen that Agathocles and men like him, after countless betrayals and cruelties, could live long and secure in their own country, defend themselves against foreign enemies, and never face a conspiracy from their own citizens — while many others, using cruelty, could not hold their states even in peacetime, let alone in the uncertain times of war. I believe it comes down to cruelties badly used or well used. Well used we may call those — if it is permissible to speak well of evil — that are done at a single stroke, out of the necessity of securing oneself, and then not persisted in, but converted into the greatest usefulness to the subjects that they can be. Badly used are those which, though few at the start, grow with time instead of dying out. Those who take the first way can, with God and with men, find some remedy for their position, as Agathocles did; for the others, it is impossible to hold on.

So it should be noted that in seizing a state, the man who takes it should run through all the injuries he will need to commit, and commit them all at once, so as not to have to renew them every day — and then, by not renewing them, reassure men and win them over with benefits. Whoever does otherwise, out of timidity or bad advice, has to keep the knife in his hand forever; and he can never lean on his subjects, since their fresh and continual injuries keep them from ever trusting him. For injuries should be done all together, so that, being tasted less, they offend less; benefits should be handed out little by little, so that they are savored longer.

And above all, a prince should live with his subjects in such a way that no accident, good or bad, forces him to change course; because when hard times bring the necessity, you are too late for the evil, and the good you do buys you nothing — it is judged forced, and earns you no thanks at all.

But coming to the other case — when a leading private citizen becomes prince of his native city not by crime or any intolerable violence but by the favor of his fellow citizens — this can be called a civil principality. Reaching it does not take pure virtù or pure fortune; it takes, rather, a kind of lucky cunning. I say a man rises to this principality by the favor of the people or by the favor of the nobles. For these two opposed humors are found in every city, and they arise from this: the people do not want to be ruled or oppressed by the nobles, and the nobles want to rule and oppress the people. From these two appetites, one of three effects follows in a city: principality, liberty, or license.

A principality is set up either by the people or by the nobles, depending on which of the two gets its chance. When the nobles see they cannot hold out against the people, they begin building up the reputation of one of their own and make him prince, so that under his shadow they can satisfy their appetite. The people likewise, seeing they cannot hold out against the nobles, build up the reputation of one man and make him prince, to be defended by his authority. The man who comes to the principality with the nobles' help holds it with more difficulty than the one who comes to it with the people's, because he finds himself prince surrounded by many who think themselves his equals — and for that reason he can neither command them nor manage them his own way. But the man who reaches the principality by popular favor finds himself alone at the top, with no one around him, or almost no one, who is not ready to obey.

Beyond that, you cannot satisfy the nobles honestly and without wronging others, but you can satisfy the people that way — because the people's aim is more decent than the nobles': the nobles want to oppress, and the people only want not to be oppressed. Add to this that against a hostile people a prince can never make himself safe, because there are too many of them; against the nobles he can, because they are few. The worst a prince can expect from a hostile people is to be abandoned by them. From hostile nobles he must fear not only abandonment but attack; for the nobles see further and move earlier, they always act in time to save themselves, and they court favor with whichever side they expect to win. And besides, the prince has to live with the same people always, but he can do perfectly well without the same nobles, since he can make them and unmake them every day, and give or take away their standing as he pleases.

To make this part clearer, I say the nobles should be considered in two main ways: either they run their course so as to bind themselves entirely to your fortune, or they do not. Those who bind themselves, and are not greedy, should be honored and loved. Those who do not bind themselves come in two kinds. If they hold back out of faint-heartedness — a natural shortage of spine — then make use of them, especially the ones with good counsel in them; in prosperity they do you honor, and in adversity you have nothing to fear from them. But when they keep clear of you deliberately, for reasons of ambition, it is a sign they are thinking more of themselves than of you; and against those a prince must guard himself, and fear them as if they were declared enemies, because in adversity they will always help bring him down.

Therefore, one who becomes prince by the favor of the people must keep the people his friend — which is easy, since all they ask is not to be oppressed. But one who becomes prince against the people, by the favor of the nobles, must before anything else try to win the people over — also easy, once he takes them under his protection. And because men, when they receive good from someone they expected only harm from, bind themselves all the more tightly to their benefactor, the people become better disposed toward him at once than if he had been raised by their own favor. A prince can win them in many ways, but the ways vary so much with circumstance that no fixed rule can be given, and I will leave them out. I will conclude only this: a prince must have the people friendly — otherwise, in adversity, he has no remedy.

Nabis, Prince of the Spartans, withstood the siege of all Greece and of a triumphant Roman army, and against them defended his country and his own rule; and when the danger came, all he needed was to secure himself against a few — which would not have been enough if the people had been his enemy. And let no one counter this opinion of mine with the worn proverb that 'he who builds on the people builds on mud.' That is true when a private citizen lays his foundation there and lets himself believe the people will rescue him when his enemies or the magistrates come for him; in that case a man will often find himself deceived, as the Gracchi were in Rome and Messer Giorgio Scali was in Florence. But if it is a prince who builds on the people — one who can command, a man of spirit, unshaken in adversity, who does not neglect his other preparations, and who keeps the whole city's nerve up by his own courage and his own orders — he will never find himself betrayed by them, and he will find he has built on solid ground.

These principalities usually come into danger at the moment they are climbing from the civil order to the absolute one. For these princes rule either in their own person or through magistrates. In the second case their position is weaker and more dangerous, because it rests entirely on the will of the citizens who hold the magistracies — and they, especially in hard times, can take the state from him with great ease, either by moving against him or simply by not obeying. And in the middle of the danger there is no time for the prince to seize absolute authority: citizens and subjects who are used to taking their orders from the magistrates are not about to obey his in that crisis, and in uncertain times he will always be short of men he can trust. A prince like this cannot build on what he sees in quiet times, when the citizens need the state — then everyone runs to him, everyone promises, and with death nowhere in sight, everyone is ready to die for him. But in hard times, when the state needs its citizens, few are to be found. And this experiment is all the more dangerous because it can only be run once. So a wise prince must think of a way to make his citizens need the state and need him — always, in every kind of weather. Then they will always be faithful.

In examining the qualities of these principalities, there is one more question to consider: whether a prince has a state strong enough to stand on its own at need, or whether he will always need someone else's protection. To make the point clearer, I say that in my judgment those princes can stand on their own who have enough men or enough money to put together a proper army and meet in the field whoever comes to attack them; and those always need others who cannot take the field against the enemy, but are forced to fall back behind their walls and defend them. The first case has been discussed, and later I will say whatever more it needs. In the second case there is nothing to say except to urge such princes to fortify and provision their own town, and to take no account of the countryside. Whoever has fortified his town well, and has handled his subjects in the way described above and to be described again, will never be attacked except with great hesitation; for men are always wary of ventures where the difficulty is plain to see, and no one sees an easy target in a prince whose town is strong and whose people do not hate him.

The cities of Germany are completely free, they have little surrounding territory, and they obey the emperor when they choose to; they fear neither him nor any other power near them, because they are fortified in such a way that everyone reckons taking them would be slow, grinding work. They all have proper moats and walls; they have artillery enough; they keep enough in the public stores to eat, drink, and burn for a year. Beyond that — to keep the common people fed without cost to the public — they always hold in common a year's worth of work to give out in the trades that are the nerve and life of the city, the industries the people live by. They keep military exercises in good repute, and have many ordinances besides to maintain them.

So a prince who has a strong city and does not make himself hated cannot be attacked; and even if someone did attack him, the attacker would leave in disgrace — because the affairs of this world are so changeable that it is next to impossible to sit idle with an army for a whole year while you besiege him. And to whoever answers that if the people have their property outside the walls and watch it burn, they will lose patience, and the long siege and their own self-interest will make them forget the prince — I reply that a powerful and spirited prince will always get past those difficulties: now giving his subjects hope that the evil will not last long, now stoking fear of the enemy's cruelty, now deftly securing himself against the ones who seem too bold.

Besides, the enemy will naturally burn and wreck the countryside on arrival, while the defenders' blood is still hot and willing; so the prince has all the less reason to worry, because after a few days, when tempers have cooled, the damage is already done, the losses already taken, and there is no undoing them. And then the people close ranks with their prince all the more, feeling he is now obliged to them, their houses burned and their lands ruined in his defense. For it is the nature of men to be bound by the benefits they give as much as by the benefits they receive. So all things considered, it will not be hard for a prudent prince to keep his citizens' minds firm through a siege, from first day to last — so long as they lack neither food nor the means to fight.

It remains now only to speak of ecclesiastical principalities. With these, every difficulty comes before you possess them: they are acquired by virtù or by fortune, and kept without either, because they are sustained by the ancient institutions of religion, which have grown so powerful, and are of such a kind, that they keep their princes in power however those princes act and live. These princes alone have states and do not defend them, subjects and do not govern them; and the states, though undefended, are not taken from them, and the subjects, though ungoverned, do not care — they neither think of breaking away, nor could they. Only these principalities, then, are secure and happy. But since they are upheld by a higher cause, which the human mind cannot reach, I will say no more about them; they are raised up and maintained by God, and it would be the work of a presumptuous and reckless man to pass judgment on them.

Still, someone might ask me how it happens that the Church has risen to such greatness in temporal power — given that until Alexander the Italian powers, and not only the ones called powers but every baron and lord down to the smallest, held that temporal power cheap, and now a king of France trembles before it, and it has been able to throw him out of Italy and to ruin the Venetians. Well known as this is, I do not think it wasted effort to call some part of it back to mind.

Before Charles, King of France, came down into Italy, this country was under the rule of the Pope, the Venetians, the King of Naples, the Duke of Milan, and the Florentines. These powers had two chief anxieties: that no foreigner should enter Italy in arms, and that none of their own number should seize more territory. The two watched most closely were the Pope and the Venetians. To hold back the Venetians it took a league of all the rest, as in the defense of Ferrara; and to hold down the Pope they used the barons of Rome. Divided into two factions, Orsini and Colonnesi, the barons never lacked a pretext for disorder; standing with weapons in hand under the Pontiff's own eyes, they kept the papacy weak and sickly. Now and then a spirited pope arose — a Sixtus — but neither fortune nor wisdom could ever rid him of this nuisance. The shortness of papal lives was the cause. In the ten years an average pope reigns, he could barely beat down one of the factions; and if one pope, so to speak, had all but wiped out the Colonnesi, up came a successor who was enemy to the Orsini — which raised the Colonnesi again — and there was no time left to wipe out the Orsini. This is why the Pope's temporal powers were held in little esteem in Italy.

Then came Alexander the Sixth, who showed better than any pontiff who ever lived what a pope with money and arms could do. Using Duke Valentino as his instrument and the French invasion as his occasion, he brought about everything I described above in discussing the duke's actions. His intention was to make the duke great, not the Church; but what he did made the Church great anyway, and after his death, and the duke's ruin, the Church inherited his labors.

Then came Pope Julius, and he found the Church strong: mistress of all the Romagna, the barons of Rome crushed, the factions beaten flat under Alexander's blows — and the road open to piling up money by methods never used before Alexander's time. Julius not only continued all this but improved on it. He set out to take Bologna, to snuff out the Venetians, and to drive the French from Italy; and every one of these enterprises succeeded, with the more credit to him because he did it all to strengthen the Church and no private man. He also kept the Orsini and Colonnesi factions within the bounds in which he found them; and though there were heads among them itching to make trouble, two things held them still: the greatness of the Church, which cowed them, and the fact that they were allowed no cardinals of their own — the origin of all their disorders. These factions will never be quiet while they have cardinals, because cardinals feed the factions, in Rome and beyond, and the barons are forced to defend them: from the ambitions of prelates come the discords and tumults of the barons. So His Holiness Pope Leo has found the papacy at the height of its power; and if others made it great with arms, one may hope that he, by his goodness and his infinite other virtues, will make it greater still, and revered.

sections.label: Chapter XII
sections.title: The Kinds of Troops, and Mercenaries

segments.text: Having discussed one by one the kinds of principality I proposed at the outset, having considered in some measure why they do well or badly, and having shown the methods by which so many men have tried to win and hold them, it remains for me now to speak generally of the offense and defense that each of them may require.

I said above that a prince must have solid foundations under him, or he necessarily comes to ruin. The principal foundations of all states — new, old, or mixed — are good laws and good arms. And since there cannot be good laws where there are not good arms, and where there are good arms there are bound to be good laws, I will leave the laws aside and speak of arms.

I say, then, that the arms with which a prince defends his state are either his own, or they are mercenary, auxiliary, or mixed. Mercenaries and auxiliaries are useless and dangerous. If a man rests his state on mercenary arms, he will never stand firm or safe; for they are disunited, ambitious, undisciplined, disloyal — swaggering among friends, cowardly before the enemy; no fear of God, no faith with men. Your ruin is put off only as long as the assault is put off: in peace you are stripped by them, in war by the enemy. The reason is that they have no love for you, and no cause to keep them in the field beyond a little pay — which is not enough to make them want to die for you. They are delighted to be your soldiers while you are not making war; when war comes, they desert or run. It should cost me little effort to prove this, since the ruin of Italy has been caused by nothing else than her resting all her hopes, for so many years, on mercenary arms. They did once make headway for certain men, and they looked brave enough against one another; but when the foreigner came, they showed what they were. So it was that Charles, King of France, was allowed to take Italy with a piece of chalk; and the man who said our sins were the cause of it told the truth — only they were not the sins he meant, but the ones I have described. And since they were the sins of princes, it is the princes who have paid the penalty.

I want to show the wretchedness of these arms more fully. Mercenary captains are either excellent soldiers or they are not. If they are, you cannot trust them: they will always be working toward greatness of their own, either by crushing you, their master, or by crushing others against your intent. And if the captain is no good, he ruins you in the ordinary way — by losing.

If the answer is that anyone with arms in hand will act this way, mercenary or not, I reply: arms are wielded either by a prince or by a republic. The prince should go in person, and do the captain's job himself. The republic must send its own citizens; when it sends a man who proves worthless, it must replace him, and when it sends a good one, it must bind him with laws so that he does not overstep the mark. Experience shows princes acting alone, and republics armed with their own arms, making enormous progress, and mercenary arms doing nothing but damage. And a republic armed with its own arms is far harder to bring under the rule of one of its citizens than a republic armed with foreign arms. Rome and Sparta stood armed and free for centuries. The Swiss are the best-armed people alive, and the freest.

As for ancient examples of mercenaries, there are the Carthaginians, who at the end of the first war with Rome were nearly crushed by their own mercenary soldiers, though the Carthaginians had their own citizens for captains. After the death of Epaminondas, the Thebans made Philip of Macedon captain of their forces; and after he had won, he took away their liberty.

When Duke Filippo died, the Milanese hired Francesco Sforza against the Venetians. He beat the enemy at Caravaggio — and then joined with the enemy to crush the Milanese, his employers. Sforza his father, in the pay of Queen Johanna of Naples, abandoned her defenseless in a stroke, so that to save her kingdom she had to throw herself into the arms of the King of Aragon. And if the Venetians and the Florentines did once enlarge their dominions with such arms, and their captains did not make themselves princes but defended them, I answer that in this the Florentines were favored by chance. Of the able captains they had cause to fear, some did not win, some met opposition, and some turned their ambition elsewhere. The one who did not win was Giovanni Acuto; and since he did not win, his loyalty was never put to the proof — but everyone will grant that had he won, the Florentines stood at his discretion. Sforza always had the Bracceschi against him, and each kept watch on the other; Francesco turned his ambition on Lombardy, Braccio against the Church and the kingdom of Naples. But come to what happened only yesterday. The Florentines made Pagolo Vitelli their captain, a very shrewd man who from private life had risen to great renown. If he had taken Pisa, no one can deny that the Florentines would have been bound to him: had he gone over to their enemies, they had no defense, and so long as they kept him, they had to obey him. As for the Venetians, look at their record, and you will see that they acted safely and gloriously so long as they made war with their own men — this was before they turned to enterprises on land — when gentlemen and armed commoners together fought with the greatest virtù. The moment they began to fight on land, they abandoned this virtù and took up the customs of Italy. In the early days of their expansion on land, having little territory there and a great reputation, they had little to fear from their captains; but as they expanded — under Carmignuola — they got a taste of the mistake. They had seen how supremely able he was; under his command they had beaten the Duke of Milan. But they also saw how cold he had grown toward the war, and they judged that with him they could win no longer, because he had no wish to win; yet they could not dismiss him, or they would lose again what they had gained. So, to secure themselves against him, they were forced to murder him. Since then they have had for captains Bartolomeo da Bergamo, Roberto da San Severino, the count of Pitigliano, and the like — men under whom the fear was of loss, not the hope of gain; as happened later at Vaila, where in one day's battle they lost what eight hundred years of hard labor had won them. From these arms come conquests that are slow, late, and feeble; and losses that are sudden and astonishing.

And since these examples have brought me to Italy, ruled now for many years by mercenary arms, I want to trace them from further back, so that once their origin and course are in view they can be better corrected. You must understand, then, how in recent times, as soon as the Empire began to be pushed out of Italy and the Pope gained more standing in temporal affairs, Italy broke up into more states. Many of the great cities took up arms against their nobles, who, favored by the emperor, had held them down, while the Church favored the cities to build its temporal power; and in many other cities, citizens rose to be princes. So Italy fell largely into the hands of the Church and of certain republics; and the Church being priests and the republics being citizens unaccustomed to arms, both began to hire foreigners.

The first to give this soldiery a reputation was Alberigo da Conio, of the Romagna. From his school came, among others, Braccio and Sforza, who in their day were the arbiters of Italy. After them came all the other captains who down to our own times have commanded the arms of Italy — and the sum of all their virtù is that Italy has been overrun by Charles, plundered by Louis, violated by Ferdinand, and insulted by the Swiss. Their method was this: first, to raise their own standing, they destroyed the standing of the infantry. They did it because, having no state of their own and living off their trade, a few foot soldiers gave them no reputation and many were more than they could feed; so they kept to cavalry, where a manageable number could be both fed and honored. Matters came to the point where in an army of twenty thousand soldiers you would not find two thousand foot. Beyond this, they had used every device to spare themselves and their soldiers hardship and fear: in the skirmishes they did not kill one another, but took prisoners and freed them without ransom; they made no assault on towns by night, and the men in the towns made none on the camps; they built neither stockade nor ditch around their quarters; they did not campaign in winter. All of this their military code permitted, and all of it, as I have said, they invented to escape hardship and danger — until they had brought Italy to slavery and contempt.

sections.label: Chapter XIII
sections.title: Auxiliaries, Mixed Troops, and One's Own

segments.text: Auxiliaries — the other useless kind of arms — are what you have when you call in a powerful outsider to come with his forces to aid you and defend you, as Pope Julius did in recent memory. Having seen in the Ferrara campaign what a sorry showing his mercenaries made, he turned to auxiliaries, and arranged with Ferdinand, King of Spain, to help him with his men and armies. These arms can be useful and good in themselves, but for the man who calls them in they are almost always ruinous: if they lose, you are undone; if they win, you are their prisoner.

Ancient histories are full of such examples, but I will stay with this fresh one of Pope Julius the Second, whose choice could hardly have been less considered: to get Ferrara, he put himself entirely into a foreigner's hands. Only his good fortune brought forth a third outcome, so that he did not reap the fruit of his bad choice. His auxiliaries were routed at Ravenna; then the Swiss rose up and — against every expectation, his own and everyone else's — chased out the victors. So he ended prisoner neither of his enemies, who had fled, nor of his auxiliaries, since the winning had been done by arms other than theirs.
The Florentines, having no arms at all of their own, brought ten thousand Frenchmen to take Pisa; and by that policy they ran more danger than at any other moment of their troubles.

The Emperor of Constantinople, to oppose his neighbors, put ten thousand Turks into Greece; and when the war was over, they would not leave. That was the beginning of Greece's servitude to the infidel.

So: the man who wants to make sure he cannot win should use these arms. They are far more dangerous than mercenaries, because with them the ruin comes ready-made: they are all one body, and all obedient to someone other than you. Mercenaries, even once they have won, need more time and a better opening to hurt you: they are not one body, and you raised them and you pay them; the outsider you set at their head cannot at once take enough authority to do you damage. In short — with mercenaries the deadliest thing is their cowardice; with auxiliaries, their virtù. Wise princes have therefore always shunned these arms and turned to their own, and have preferred to lose with their own men rather than win with another's, judging no victory real that is won with borrowed arms.

I will never hesitate to cite Cesare Borgia and his actions. This duke entered the Romagna with auxiliary arms, bringing in nothing but French soldiers, and with them he took Imola and Forli. When those arms then struck him as unsafe, he turned to mercenaries, judging the danger there smaller, and hired the Orsini and the Vitelli. Finding these, in the handling, doubtful, disloyal, and dangerous, he destroyed them, and turned to his own men. And the difference between these kinds of arms is easily seen by considering the difference in the duke's reputation when he had the French, when he had the Orsini and Vitelli, and when he stood on his own soldiers and on himself. His reputation grew at every step; and he was never rated so high as when everyone saw that he was complete master of his own forces.

I meant not to go beyond Italian and recent examples, but I am unwilling to leave out Hiero the Syracusan, since he is one of those I named above. Made head of the army by the Syracusans, as I said, he saw at once that mercenary soldiery was useless — its captains were built just like our Italian condottieri. And concluding that he could neither keep them nor let them go, he had them all cut to pieces; after which he made war with his own arms, and not with anyone else's.

I want to recall, too, a figure from the Old Testament made for this subject. When David offered himself to Saul to go and fight Goliath, the Philistine champion, Saul, to give him heart, dressed him in his own armor — and David, once he had it on, refused it, saying he could not give a true account of himself in it: he would meet the enemy with his sling and his knife. In the end, the armor of others falls off your back, or weighs you down, or binds you tight.

Charles the Seventh, father of King Louis the Eleventh, having freed France from the English by his fortune and his virtù, understood this necessity of arming himself with his own arms, and set up in his kingdom the ordinances of the men-at-arms and the infantry. Then his son King Louis abolished the infantry and began to hire the Swiss — a mistake which, followed by others, is now plainly seen to be the source of that kingdom's dangers. For by raising the reputation of the Swiss, he degraded all his own arms: the infantry he wiped out altogether, and his men-at-arms he made dependent on the arms of others, since, being accustomed to fight alongside the Swiss, they no longer believe they can win without them. Hence the French are not enough against the Swiss, and without the Swiss they do not attempt much against anyone else. The armies of France, then, have been mixed — part mercenary, part her own; arms which, taken together, are much better than pure auxiliaries or pure mercenaries, and much inferior to one's own. The example already given is enough: the kingdom of France would be unbeatable today if the ordinance of Charles had been enlarged, or even kept.

But the small wisdom of men will begin a thing that tastes good at the time and never notice the poison underneath — as I said earlier about wasting fevers. The ruler of a principality who does not recognize evils at their birth is not truly wise; and that is given to few. And if you look for the first cause of the ruin of the Roman Empire, you will find it was nothing but the hiring of the Goths: from that beginning the strength of the Roman Empire started to slacken, and all the virtù that drained out of it was handed to them.

I conclude, then, that no principality is secure without arms of its own; it is instead wholly dependent on fortune, having no virtù to defend it faithfully in adversity. And it was ever the opinion and verdict of wise men that nothing is so weak or so unstable as a reputation for power that does not rest on strength of one's own. And one's own arms are those composed of subjects, or of citizens, or of dependents of yours: all others are mercenary or auxiliary. The way to organize your own arms is easily found if you go back over the arrangements of the four men I have named, and if you see how Philip, father of Alexander the Great, and how many republics and princes have armed and ordered themselves. To their methods I defer entirely.

sections.label: Chapter XIV
sections.title: The Prince and the Art of War

segments.text: A prince, then, should have no other object, no other thought, and take nothing else for his craft, but war, its rules, and its discipline; for that is the only art expected of the man who commands. And it is an art of such virtù that it not only keeps in place those who were born princes, but many times lifts men from private station to that rank — while the reverse is also on record: princes who thought more of luxury than of arms have lost their states. The first thing that loses you your state is neglect of this art; the thing that wins you a state is mastery of it. Francesco Sforza, because he was armed, rose from private citizen to Duke of Milan; his sons, because they fled the hardships of arms, sank from dukes to private citizens. For among the other evils that being unarmed brings you, it makes you despised — one of those disgraces, as will be said below, that a prince must guard against. Between an armed man and an unarmed man there is no proportion at all; and it is not reasonable that the armed should obey the unarmed willingly, or that the unarmed should be safe among armed servants. With disdain on one side and suspicion on the other, they cannot work well together. So a prince who understands nothing of war, beyond the other miseries already mentioned, cannot be respected by his soldiers, and cannot trust them. He should never, therefore, lift his thoughts from the exercise of war; and he should exercise it harder in peace than in war. He can do this in two ways: with action, and with the mind.

As for action: besides keeping his men well ordered and well drilled, he should live in the hunt, hardening his body to exertion and learning the nature of ground as he goes — how the mountains rise, how the valleys open, how the plains lie; what the rivers and marshes are like — and in this he should take the greatest care. The knowledge pays twice. First, he learns to know his own country, and can better see how to defend it. Second, by knowing that terrain and having it under his feet, he grasps with ease any new terrain he must scout; for the hills, valleys, plains, rivers, and marshes of Tuscany, say, bear a certain resemblance to those of other provinces, so that from knowing the ground of one province you come easily to know the ground of others. And the prince who lacks this skill lacks the first quality a captain must have; for it is what teaches you to find your enemy, choose your quarters, lead armies, order a battle, and lay siege to towns with the advantage on your side.

Philopoemen, prince of the Achaeans, among the praises writers have given him, is praised for this: that in peacetime he never thought about anything but the ways of war. When he was in the country with friends, he would often stop and reason with them: "If the enemy were on that hill and we stood here with our army, which of us would have the advantage? How could we go at them, keeping formation? If we wanted to retreat, how would we manage it? If they retreated, how should we pursue?" And as he went he would set before them every chance that can befall an army; he heard their opinions, gave his own, and backed it with reasons — so that, through this endless rehearsal, no accident could ever arise, with his armies in the field, for which he did not have the remedy.

As for exercising the mind, the prince should read histories, and study in them the actions of excellent men: see how they carried themselves in war; examine the causes of their victories and their defeats, so as to flee the one and imitate the other; and above all, do as some excellent man before him has done — take as his model some earlier man who was praised and glorified, and keep that man's deeds and actions always by him, as Alexander the Great is said to have imitated Achilles; Caesar, Alexander; Scipio, Cyrus. And whoever reads the life of Cyrus written by Xenophon will then recognize, in the life of Scipio, how much glory that imitation earned him, and how closely, in chastity, affability, humanity, and generosity, Scipio kept to what Xenophon wrote of Cyrus. Such are the ways a wise prince must observe; and he should never stand idle in peaceful times, but work in them industriously to build up capital he can draw on in adversity — so that when fortune turns, she finds him ready to resist her.

sections.label: Chapter XV
sections.title: What Princes Are Praised or Blamed For

segments.text: It remains now to see what the conduct and bearing of a prince ought to be toward his subjects and his friends. And because I know that many have written on this, I fear that in writing on it too I will be thought presumptuous — the more so because in treating the matter I depart from the paths laid down by others. But since my intention is to write something useful to whoever understands it, it has seemed to me more fitting to go straight after the effectual truth of the thing than after the imagination of it. Many have imagined republics and principalities that no one has ever seen or known to exist in the world as it is; for the way men live is so far from the way men ought to live that whoever lets go of what is done for what ought to be done learns his ruin sooner than his preservation. A man who insists on being good in everything must come to ruin among so many who are not good.

So it is necessary for a prince who wants to keep his state to learn how not to be good, and to use that knowledge, or not use it, as necessity requires. Setting aside, then, the things imagined about a prince, and speaking of the things that are true, I say that all men, whenever they are spoken of — and princes most of all, being set so high — are marked with some one of those qualities that draw blame or praise. One is held generous, another a miser — I use the Tuscan word, since in our tongue an avaricious man is still one who craves to get by plunder, while we call a miser the man who holds back too hard from using what is his own; one is a giver, another grasping; one cruel, another merciful; one a breaker of faith, another a keeper of it; one effeminate and cowardly, another fierce and full of spirit; one humane, another haughty; one lecherous, another chaste; one straightforward, another sly; one hard, another easygoing; one grave, another frivolous; one religious, another unbelieving; and so on. And I know that everyone will admit it would be a most praiseworthy thing for a prince to possess, of all the qualities named above, the ones held to be good. But since they cannot all be had, nor all wholly practiced — the conditions of human life do not allow it — a prince must be prudent enough to know how to escape the infamy of those vices that would take his state from him, and to guard, if he can, against the vices that would not; and if he cannot, he may let those go with less concern. And further, he must not care about incurring infamy for vices without which the state can hardly be saved; because, when everything is weighed, he will find some things that look like virtue and would be his ruin if he followed them, and others that look like vice and bring him, if he follows them, his security and his well-being.

Beginning, then, with the first of the qualities named above, I say that it would be good to be thought generous. Nevertheless, generosity practiced in such a way that you get the name for it does you harm; for if it is practiced virtuously, and as it ought to be practiced, it will not be known, and you will not escape the infamy of its opposite. And so a man who wants to keep up the name of generous among men cannot leave out any kind of lavish display; a prince of that sort will consume his whole substance in such displays, and in the end, if he wants to keep the name of generous, he will be forced to burden his people beyond measure, to squeeze them with taxes, and to do everything that can be done to raise money. This will begin to make him hateful to his subjects and, as he grows poor, little regarded by anyone; so that, having offended the many with this generosity of his and rewarded the few, he feels the first pinch of trouble and totters at the first real danger; and when he recognizes this and tries to pull back, he runs at once into the infamy of a miser.

A prince, then, since he cannot practice this virtue of generosity in a way that is recognized without hurting himself, ought, if he is prudent, not to mind being called a miser. With time he will be thought more and more generous, once men see that his thrift makes his revenues sufficient, that he can defend himself against whoever makes war on him, and that he can undertake campaigns without burdening his people — so that he ends up practicing generosity toward all those from whom he takes nothing, who are countless, and miserliness toward all those to whom he gives nothing, who are few.

In our times we have not seen great things done except by those who were held miserly; the rest were wiped out. Pope Julius the Second, though he made use of a name for generosity to reach the papacy, did not try to keep it afterward, because he wanted to be able to make war on the King of France; and he waged all his wars without laying any extraordinary tax on his subjects, because his long thrift covered the extra expense. The present King of Spain, if he had been held generous, would not have undertaken or won so many campaigns. A prince, then, so long as he does not have to rob his subjects, can defend himself, is not forced into poverty and contempt, and is not driven to become rapacious, ought to count the name of miser for little, since it is one of the vices that make his rule possible.

And if someone says: Caesar rose to empire through his generosity, and many others have reached the highest ranks because they were generous and were held to be so — I answer: either you are already a prince, or you are on the way to becoming one. In the first case this generosity is harmful; in the second it is quite necessary to be thought generous. And Caesar was one of those trying to reach the rule of Rome; but if, after reaching it, he had lived on and had not moderated his spending, he would have destroyed that empire. And if someone replies: many who were held most generous have been princes and have done great things with their armies — I answer: a prince spends either what is his own and his subjects', or what belongs to others. In the first case he ought to be sparing; in the second he ought not to leave out any part of generosity. For the prince who marches with his armies, living on plunder, sack, and ransom, is handling other men's property, and there this openhandedness is necessary — without it his soldiers would not follow him. With what is not yours or your subjects' you can be a freer giver, as Cyrus, Caesar, and Alexander were; for spending what belongs to others takes away none of your reputation but adds to it; only spending your own hurts you.

And there is nothing that consumes itself the way generosity does: while you practice it, you lose the power to practice it, and you become either poor and despised or, to escape poverty, rapacious and hated. And among all the things a prince must guard against is being despised and hated — and generosity leads you to both. So it is wiser to keep the name of miser, which breeds an infamy without hatred, than, by straining after the name of generous, to be forced into the name of rapacious, which breeds an infamy with hatred.

sections.label: Chapter XVII
sections.title: Cruelty and Mercy: Loved or Feared

segments.text: Coming now to the other qualities named before, I say that every prince ought to want to be held merciful and not cruel; nevertheless, he must take care not to use this mercy badly. Cesare Borgia was held cruel; and yet that cruelty of his mended the Romagna, united it, and brought it back to peace and loyalty. Looked at closely, he will be seen to have been far more merciful than the Florentine people, who, to escape a name for cruelty, let Pistoia be destroyed. A prince, then, ought not to mind the infamy of cruelty when it keeps his subjects united and loyal; for with a very few exemplary punishments he will be more merciful than those who, out of too much mercy, let disorders run on until they end in killings and plunder — for these hurt a whole community, while the executions that come from a prince hurt only a single man.

And of all princes, it is the new prince who cannot escape the name of cruel, since new states are full of dangers. Hence Virgil, through Dido's mouth, excuses the inhumanity of her rule by the fact that it was new, saying:
Res dura, et regni novitas me talia cogunt moliri, et late fines custode tueri.
Hard necessity, and the newness of my kingdom, force me to such measures — to guard my borders far and wide with sentries.

Nevertheless, he should be slow to believe and slow to act, and should not conjure fears for himself; he should proceed in a temperate way, with prudence and humanity, so that too much confidence does not make him incautious and too much distrust does not make him unbearable.

From this a dispute arises: whether it is better to be loved than feared, or the reverse. The answer is that one would want to be both; but since it is hard to combine them, it is much safer to be feared than loved, if one of the two must be given up. For this can be said of men generally: they are ungrateful, fickle, pretenders and dissemblers, quick to run from danger, greedy for gain; and while you are doing them good they are entirely yours — they offer you their blood, their property, their lives, their children, as I said above, so long as the need is far off; but when it comes near, they turn away. And the prince who has rested entirely on their words, and finds himself bare of other preparations, is ruined; for friendships bought at a price, and not with greatness and nobility of spirit, are paid for but not owned, and at the moment of need they cannot be spent. And men have less hesitation about harming one who makes himself loved than one who makes himself feared; for love is held by a chain of obligation which, men being wretched, is broken at every turn of their own advantage; but fear is held by a dread of punishment that never lets you go.

Nevertheless, a prince should make himself feared in such a way that, if he does not win love, he escapes hatred; for being feared and not being hated go together very well. And he will always manage this if he keeps his hands off the property of his citizens and his subjects, and off their women. And when he does have to proceed against someone's life, he should do it where there is proper justification and manifest cause; but above all he must keep off other men's property, for men forget the death of a father more quickly than the loss of a patrimony. Besides, pretexts for taking property are never lacking: a man who begins to live by plunder will always find a reason to seize what belongs to someone else; whereas reasons for taking a life are rarer, and give out sooner. But when a prince is with his armies and has a multitude of soldiers under his command, then it is absolutely necessary not to care about the name of cruel, for without that name no army was ever kept united or fit for any action.

Among Hannibal's admirable actions this one is counted: that though he led an enormous army, a mixture of countless races of men, to fight in foreign lands, no dissension ever arose in it — not among the men, and not against their leader — in bad fortune or in good. This could come from nothing but his inhuman cruelty, which, together with his boundless virtù, made him always revered and terrible in his soldiers' eyes; and without it, his other virtù would not have been enough to produce that effect. Writers who have thought about this too little admire his achievement on the one hand and condemn its chief cause on the other. And that his other virtù would not have sufficed can be seen in Scipio — a man of the rarest kind, not only in his own times but in the whole memory of human affairs — whose armies mutinied against him in Spain. That came from nothing but his excessive leniency, which had given his soldiers more license than fits military discipline. Fabius Maximus threw it in his face in the Senate and called him the corrupter of the Roman soldiery. The Locrians, after one of Scipio's legates had wrecked them, went unavenged by him, and the legate's insolence went uncorrected — all of it born of that easy nature of his; so that when someone in the Senate wanted to excuse him, he said there were many men who knew better how to avoid erring themselves than how to correct the errors of others. In time that nature would have stained Scipio's fame and glory, had he kept command long enough; but living under the government of the Senate, this damaging quality of his not only stayed hidden but brought him glory.

I conclude, then, returning to being feared and loved: since men love at their own pleasure and fear at the pleasure of the prince, a wise prince should build on what is his own, not on what belongs to others; he must only contrive to escape hatred, as was said.

sections.label: Chapter XVIII
sections.title: How Princes Should Keep Their Word

segments.text: Everyone understands how praiseworthy it is in a prince to keep his word and to live with integrity and not by cunning. Nevertheless, experience in our own times shows that the princes who have done great things are the ones who have held their word cheap, who have known how to run rings around men's wits with cunning — and in the end they have beaten the ones who founded themselves on honesty. You must know, then, that there are two ways of fighting: one with laws, the other with force. The first is proper to man, the second to beasts; but because the first is often not enough, one must have recourse to the second. So a prince needs to know how to use both the beast and the man well. This point was taught to princes under cover by the ancient writers, who tell how Achilles and many other princes of antiquity were given to Chiron the centaur to be raised and brought up under his discipline. Having a half-beast, half-man for a teacher means nothing else than this: a prince needs to know how to use both natures, and the one does not last without the other. Since a prince is forced, then, to know how to use the beast well, he should pick from among the beasts the fox and the lion; for the lion cannot defend himself from snares, and the fox cannot defend himself from wolves. So one must be a fox to recognize the snares, and a lion to frighten off the wolves. Those who stand simply on the lion do not understand their business. A prudent lord, therefore, cannot keep his word — and should not — when keeping it works against him and when the reasons that made him promise are gone. If men were all good, this precept would not be good; but because they are wretched, and would not keep their word to you, you need not keep yours to them. Nor has a prince ever lacked legitimate grounds with which to color over his breach of faith. Of this one could give countless modern examples, and show how many peace treaties and how many promises have been made void and empty by the faithlessness of princes; and the one who has known best how to use the fox has come out best.

But this nature has to be painted over well: one must be a great pretender and dissembler. And men are so simple, and so obedient to the necessities of the moment, that the deceiver will always find someone willing to be deceived. Of recent examples I will not keep silent about one. Alexander the Sixth never did anything else, never thought about anything else, than deceiving men, and he always found subjects it could be done to. Never was there a man with greater force in asserting a thing, or who affirmed it with heavier oaths and kept it less; and yet his deceptions always came off exactly as he wished, because he knew this side of the world so well.

A prince, then, need not actually have all the qualities listed above, but he very much needs to appear to have them. Indeed, I will dare to say this: that having them and observing them always is harmful, and appearing to have them is useful — to appear merciful, faithful, humane, upright, religious, and to be so; but with your mind so built that, if you need not to be so, you can and do know how to change into the contrary.

And this has to be understood: a prince, and especially a new prince, cannot observe all the things for which men are called good, since to maintain his state he is often forced to act against faith, against charity, against humanity, against religion. So he needs a mind ready to turn as the winds of fortune and the shifting of things command him; and, as I said above, not to depart from good while he can, but to know how to enter into evil when he has to.

A prince must therefore take great care that nothing ever falls from his mouth that is not full of the five qualities named above, so that to see him and hear him he seems all mercy, all faith, all integrity, all humanity, all religion. And nothing is more necessary to appear to have than this last quality. Men in general judge more by the eye than by the hand; for everyone gets to see you, few get to touch you. Everyone sees what you appear to be; few feel what you are, and those few do not dare set themselves against the opinion of the many, who have the majesty of the state defending them. And in the actions of all men, and most of all of princes, where there is no court of appeal, one looks to the outcome.

So let a prince win and hold his state: the means will always be judged honorable, and everyone will praise them; because the crowd is taken by appearances and by the way a thing comes out — and in the world there is no one but the crowd; the few find no footing when the many have something to lean on.

A certain prince of the present time, whom it is better not to name, never preaches anything but peace and good faith, and he is the bitterest enemy of both; and if he had ever observed either one, it would more than once have cost him his reputation or his state.

Now that I have spoken of the most important of the qualities mentioned above, I want to run briefly through the others under this general heading: that the prince should attend, as was partly said above, to avoiding the things that make him hated or held in contempt. Whenever he avoids these, he will have done his part, and he will find no danger at all in his other bad names.

What makes him hated above everything, as I said, is to be rapacious — a usurper of the property and the women of his subjects. From these he must keep away: whenever you take neither property nor honor from the generality of men, they live content, and you have only to contend with the ambition of the few, which can be checked easily, and in many ways.

What makes him contemptible is to be held changeable, frivolous, effeminate, faint-hearted, irresolute. A prince must guard against these as a ship guards against a reef, and contrive that in his actions men recognize greatness, spirit, gravity, and strength; and concerning the private dealings of his subjects, he should insist that his sentence be irrevocable, and keep up such an opinion of himself that no one thinks of deceiving him or getting around him.

The prince who gives this impression of himself stands in high repute, and against a man of such repute conspiracy is difficult, and attack is difficult, so long as it is understood that he is excellent and revered by his own people. For a prince must have two fears: one inside, on account of his subjects; one outside, on account of foreign powers. From the outside he defends himself with good arms and good allies — and if he has good arms he will always have good allies. And things inside will always stand firm when things outside stand firm, unless a conspiracy has already disturbed them; and even if the outside does move against him, if he has ordered himself and lived as I have said, and does not lose heart, he will withstand every assault — as I said Nabis the Spartan did.

But as for his subjects, when things outside are quiet, his fear is that they may conspire in secret. From this the prince secures himself well enough by escaping hatred and contempt and keeping the people satisfied with him — which it is necessary to accomplish, as was said above at length. And among the most powerful remedies a prince has against conspiracies is precisely this: not being hated by the people at large. For whoever conspires always believes the prince's death will please the people; when he believes it will offend them, he cannot screw up the courage for such a course, because the difficulties on the conspirators' side are infinite. Experience shows that conspiracies have been many, and few have ended well. For a conspirator cannot act alone, and he can take companions only from those he believes discontented; and the moment you open your mind to a discontented man, you give him the means to content himself, since by informing on you he can hope for every kind of reward. Seeing sure gain on that side, and on the other nothing but doubt and danger, he must be either a rare friend to you, or an utterly implacable enemy of the prince, to keep faith with you.

And to put the thing briefly, I say that on the conspirator's side there is nothing but fear, jealousy, and the prospect of punishment, which terrifies him; but on the prince's side there is the majesty of the principality, the laws, the protection of friends and of the state, all defending him. Add to these the goodwill of the people, and it is impossible that anyone should be reckless enough to conspire. For where a conspirator ordinarily has cause to fear before the execution of his crime, in this case he must fear afterward as well — having the people for his enemy once the deed is done — and for that reason he can hope for no refuge anywhere.

On this subject one could give endless examples, but I will content myself with one, which happened within the memory of our fathers. Messer Annibale Bentivogli, grandfather of the present Messer Annibale, was prince in Bologna, and the Canneschi, conspiring against him, murdered him; no one of his line remained except Messer Giovanni, then in swaddling clothes. The moment the murder was done, the people rose up and killed all the Canneschi. This came from the goodwill the house of Bentivogli enjoyed among the people in those days — a goodwill so great that, with Annibale dead and no one of the house left in Bologna who could rule the state, the Bolognese, having word that in Florence there was a man of Bentivogli blood who until then had passed for a blacksmith's son, went to Florence to find him and gave him the government of their city; and it was governed by him until Messer Giovanni came of age to rule.

I conclude, then, that a prince should take little account of conspiracies when the people are well disposed toward him; but when the people are his enemy and hold him in hatred, he must fear everything and everyone. And well-ordered states and wise princes have taken every care not to drive the great to desperation, and to keep the people satisfied and content: for this is one of the most important matters a prince has.

Among the well-ordered and well-governed kingdoms of our times is France, and in it one finds countless good institutions on which the liberty and security of the king depend. The first of these is the Parlement — the high court — and its authority. For the man who ordered that kingdom, knowing the ambition of the powerful and their insolence, judged that they needed a bit in their mouths to hold them; and knowing on the other side the hatred, rooted in fear, that the people at large bear toward the great, and wanting to reassure them, he did not wish this to be the particular charge of the king — so as to spare him the blame he would get from the great for favoring the people, and from the people for favoring the great. So he set up a third judge, to be the one who, without any burden falling on the king, would beat down the great and favor the small. There could be no better or more prudent arrangement, nor a greater cause of the security of the king and the kingdom. From this one can draw another notable rule: that princes should have unpopular duties administered by others, and hand out the favors themselves. And again I conclude that a prince should value the great, but not make himself hated by the people.

Perhaps it will seem to some, looking at the lives and deaths of certain Roman emperors, that they are examples contrary to this opinion of mine — men who lived excellently throughout and showed great virtù of spirit, and nevertheless lost the empire, or were killed by their own men conspiring against them. Wishing to answer this objection, I will take up the qualities of some of the emperors, showing that the causes of their ruin were no different from the ones I have set out; and along the way I will put forward the things worth noting for anyone who reads the affairs of those times.

It will be enough to take all the emperors who succeeded to the empire from Marcus the philosopher down to Maximinus: these were Marcus, his son Commodus, Pertinax, Julianus, Severus, his son Antoninus Caracalla, Macrinus, Heliogabalus, Alexander, and Maximinus.

And first it is to be noted that, where in other principalities one has only to contend with the ambition of the great and the insolence of the people, the Roman emperors had a third difficulty: they had to bear with the cruelty and greed of the soldiers. This was so hard a thing that it caused the ruin of many, since it was difficult to satisfy the soldiers and the people at once. The people loved quiet, and for that reason loved unassuming princes; the soldiers loved a prince of military spirit — insolent, cruel, and rapacious — and wanted him to practice those qualities on the people, so that they could double their pay and vent their own greed and cruelty. The result was that the emperors who did not have, by nature or by art, a reputation great enough to hold both in check always came to ruin; and most of them, especially those who came to the principate as new men, once they recognized the difficulty of these two opposed humors, turned to satisfying the soldiers, counting it a small thing to injure the people. That choice was necessary: since princes cannot avoid being hated by somebody, they are bound first to try not to be hated by any whole class of their subjects; and when they cannot manage that, they must contrive with every effort to escape the hatred of the classes that are most powerful. And so those emperors who, being new men, had need of extraordinary support held to the soldiers rather than to the people — which turned out useful to them or not according to whether the prince knew how to keep his reputation up with the troops.

From these causes it followed that Marcus, Pertinax, and Alexander — all men of modest life, lovers of justice, enemies of cruelty, humane, and kind — all, except Marcus, came to a sad end. Marcus alone lived and died with the highest honor, because he succeeded to the empire by hereditary right and did not have to acknowledge it as a gift of either the soldiers or the people; and then, being furnished with many virtù that made him revered, he held both orders within their bounds as long as he lived, and was never hated or despised.

But Pertinax was made emperor against the will of the soldiers, who, being used to living licentiously under Commodus, could not stand the honest life Pertinax wanted to bring them back to; and having thus made himself hated — and with the hatred came contempt, for he was old — he was ruined at the very start of his administration. And here it must be noted that hatred is earned by good deeds as much as by bad ones; and so, as I said above, a prince who wants to hold his state is often forced not to be good. For when the body you judge you need in order to maintain yourself — the people, the soldiers, or the great — is corrupt, you must follow its humor to satisfy it, and then good deeds are your enemy.

But let us come to Alexander. He was of such goodness that among the praises given him is this: in the fourteen years he held the empire, no one was ever put to death by him without trial. Nevertheless, being held effeminate — a man who let himself be ruled by his mother — he fell into contempt for it, and the army conspired against him and killed him.

Turning now to the opposite qualities of Commodus, Severus, Antoninus Caracalla, and Maximinus: you will find them utterly cruel and utterly rapacious — men who, to satisfy their soldiers, spared the people no kind of injury. And all of them, except Severus, came to a bad end. For in Severus there was so much virtù that, by keeping the soldiers his friends, he could always reign happily even while the people were being crushed by him; his virtù made him so remarkable in the eyes of soldiers and people alike that the people stood, in a manner, dazed and stunned before him, and the soldiers reverent and satisfied. And because his actions were great, and notable in a new prince, I want to show briefly how well he knew how to play the fox and the lion — the two natures I said above a prince must imitate.

Julianus the emperor being known for his slackness, Severus persuaded the army he commanded in Slavonia that it would be right to march on Rome and avenge the death of Pertinax, whom the praetorian soldiers had killed. Under that pretext, and without showing any appetite for the empire, he moved his army against Rome, and was in Italy before his departure was even known. When he reached Rome, the Senate, out of fear, elected him emperor, and Julianus was killed. After this beginning, two obstacles remained if Severus was to master the whole state: one in Asia, where Niger, commander of the Asian armies, had had himself proclaimed emperor; the other in the west, where Albinus also aspired to the empire. And because he judged it dangerous to declare himself the enemy of both, he decided to attack Niger and deceive Albinus. To Albinus he wrote that, having been elected emperor by the Senate, he wished to share that dignity with him; he sent him the title of Caesar and had the Senate take him on as colleague — all of which Albinus accepted as true. But once Severus had defeated and killed Niger and pacified the East, he returned to Rome and complained in the Senate that Albinus, unmindful of the benefits received from him, had treacherously sought to kill him, and that he was therefore obliged to go and punish his ingratitude. He then went to find him in France, and stripped him of his state and his life. Whoever examines this man's actions in detail, then, will find a most ferocious lion and a most cunning fox; will find him feared and revered by everyone, and not hated by his armies; and will not marvel that he, a new man, was able to hold so great an empire — for his enormous reputation defended him always from the hatred the people might have conceived for his plunderings.

But his son Antoninus was also a man of the most excellent parts, which made him marvelous in the sight of the people and welcome to the soldiers: he was a military man, able to bear every hardship, contemptuous of every delicate food and every other softness, and this made all the armies love him. Nevertheless, his ferocity and cruelty were so great and so unheard of — after countless individual killings, he had put to death a great part of the people of Rome and all the people of Alexandria — that he became hateful to the whole world and began to be feared even by those he kept around him; and he was killed by a centurion in the middle of his own army. Here it is to be noted that deaths like this one, which follow from the deliberate resolve of an unshakable mind, are impossible for princes to avoid, since anyone who does not care about dying can strike the blow; but a prince may fear them less, because they are very rare. He must only keep from doing grave injury to any of those who serve him and whom he keeps close around him in the service of the state. Antoninus had not: he had shamefully killed a brother of that centurion, and threatened the man himself every day, yet kept him in his bodyguard — a reckless course, fit to ruin him, and so it did.

But let us come to Commodus, who could have held the empire with great ease, since as the son of Marcus he had it by inheritance; he had only to walk in his father's footsteps, and he would have satisfied soldiers and people alike. But being of a cruel and bestial spirit, in order to practice his rapacity on the people he set about indulging the armies and making them licentious; and on the other side, by not keeping up his own dignity — going down into the arenas again and again to fight with the gladiators, and doing other things utterly vile and unworthy of the imperial majesty — he became contemptible in the sight of the soldiers. Hated on the one side and despised on the other, he was conspired against and killed.

It remains to tell the qualities of Maximinus. He was a most warlike man; and the armies, disgusted with the softness of Alexander, whom I have discussed above, killed him and elected Maximinus to the empire. He did not keep it long, for two things made him hated and despised: one, that his origin was of the basest — he had once herded sheep in Thrace, a fact known everywhere, which lowered him enormously in every eye; the other, that at the start of his reign he put off going to Rome to take possession of the imperial seat, and meanwhile earned a name for the utmost ferocity, having through his prefects, in Rome and everywhere else in the empire, carried out many cruelties. So the whole world was stirred at once with disdain for the meanness of his blood and with hatred born of fear of his savagery; and first Africa rebelled, then the Senate with the whole people of Rome, and then all Italy conspired against him. His own army joined them: laying siege to Aquileia and finding it hard to take, disgusted with his cruelty, and fearing him less when they saw how many enemies he had, they killed him.

Of Heliogabalus, Macrinus, and Julianus I will not speak: being wholly contemptible, they were snuffed out at once. I will come instead to the close of this discourse. The princes of our own times suffer far less from this difficulty of giving the soldiers extraordinary satisfaction in their governments; for though some consideration must still be shown them, the thing is soon settled, since none of these princes keeps standing armies grown old together in the government and administration of provinces, as the armies of the Roman empire were. If it was then necessary to satisfy the soldiers before the people, it was because the soldiers could do more than the people; now it is necessary for all princes, except the Turk and the Sultan of Egypt, to satisfy the people before the soldiers, because the people can do more than they can.

I make an exception of the Turk, because he always keeps about him twelve thousand foot soldiers and fifteen thousand horse, on whom the security and strength of his kingdom depend; and it is necessary for that lord to keep them his friends, setting every other consideration of the people aside. The kingdom of the Sultan of Egypt is similar: being entirely in the hands of the soldiers, he too must keep them his friends, without regard for the people. And note that this state of the Sultan is unlike all other principalities: it resembles the Christian pontificate, which cannot be called a hereditary principality or a new principality. For it is not the sons of the old prince who inherit and remain lords, but the man raised to that rank by those who have the authority to elect him, the sons remaining noblemen only; and since this order is ancient, the state cannot be called a new principality. None of the difficulties of new ones are found in it: for though the prince is new, the orders of the state are old, and arranged to receive him as if he were their hereditary lord.

But let us return to our subject. I say that whoever considers the discourse written above will see that either hatred or contempt was the cause of the ruin of the emperors named; and he will also see how it happened that, some proceeding one way and some the contrary way, in each group one man ended happily and the rest unhappily. For Pertinax and Alexander, being new princes, it was useless and harmful to want to imitate Marcus, who stood in the principate by hereditary right; and likewise for Caracalla, Commodus, and Maximinus it was fatal to imitate Severus, since they did not have virtù enough to follow in his footsteps. So a new prince in a new principality cannot imitate the actions of Marcus, and yet has no need to follow those of Severus; rather, he should take from Severus the parts necessary to found his state, and from Marcus the parts fitting and glorious for preserving a state already established and firm.

Some princes, in order to hold their states securely, have disarmed their subjects; some have kept their subject towns divided; some have fed enmities against themselves; some have set out to win over the men they suspected at the start of their rule; some have built fortresses; some have torn them down and destroyed them. And though no fixed judgment can be passed on any of this without coming to the particulars of the state where such a decision would have to be taken, nevertheless I will speak in the broad way the matter itself allows.

There has never been a case, then, of a new prince disarming his subjects; on the contrary, whenever he has found them disarmed he has always armed them. For when you arm them, those arms become yours; the men you suspected become faithful, and the ones who were faithful stay so; and from subjects they are made into your partisans. And since all your subjects cannot be armed, when you favor the ones you do arm you can deal more securely with the rest: the difference in treatment that the armed recognize toward themselves puts them in your debt, and the others excuse you, judging it necessary that men who carry more danger and stricter obligation should have more reward. But when you disarm them, you begin to offend them: you show that you distrust them, whether for cowardice or for lack of loyalty, and either of those opinions breeds hatred against you. And because you cannot stay unarmed, you are forced to turn to mercenary soldiery, which is what was said of it above; and even were it good, it cannot be good enough to defend you against powerful enemies and suspect subjects at once. Therefore, as I have said, a new prince in a new principality has always set up arms there; the histories are full of such examples.
