But when a prince acquires a new state that is joined like a limb to his old one, then that state must be disarmed — except for the men who were your partisans in acquiring it; and those too, with time and occasion, must be made soft and effeminate, and things arranged so that the arms of your whole state are in the hands of your own soldiers, the ones who live close to you in your old state.

Our forefathers, and the men who were counted wise, used to say that Pistoia had to be held with factions and Pisa with fortresses; and on that principle they nursed quarrels in some of their subject towns, the more easily to keep hold of them. In those days, when Italy stood in a certain balance, this may have been sound practice; but I do not think it can be given as a precept today, for I do not believe divisions ever did anyone any good. On the contrary: when the enemy approaches, divided cities are inevitably lost at once, because the weaker faction will always attach itself to the outside forces, and the other will not be able to stand. The Venetians, moved, I believe, by the reasons given above, fostered the Guelf and Ghibelline sects in their subject cities; and though they never let them come to blood, they still nursed these differences among the citizens so that, being occupied with their own quarrels, they would not unite against them. Which, as we saw, did not afterward turn out to their purpose: for when they were routed at Vailà, one of the factions immediately took heart and seized their whole dominion. Such methods, besides, argue weakness in the prince; in a vigorous principality such divisions are never permitted, for they profit you only in peacetime, letting you manage your subjects more easily by their means — but when war comes, an order of this kind shows its own falsity.

Without doubt, princes become great when they overcome the difficulties and the opposition put in their way; and so fortune — above all when she wants to make a new prince great, who has more need of winning reputation than a hereditary one — raises up enemies for him and sets them on campaigns against him, so that he may have cause to overcome them and to climb higher up the very ladder his enemies have carried to him. For this reason many judge that a wise prince, when he has the occasion for it, should cunningly feed some enmity against himself, so that by crushing it his greatness rises the higher.

Princes, and especially new ones, have found more faith and more usefulness in the men they held suspect at the beginning of their rule than in those they trusted at first. Pandolfo Petrucci, prince of Siena, governed his state more with the men he had suspected than with the others. But of this one cannot speak at large, because it varies with the case. I will say only this: men who were enemies of a prince at the beginning of his rule, if they are of the kind that need support to hold their position, can always be won over with the greatest ease; and they are the more tightly bound to serve him faithfully because they know how much they need to cancel, by their deeds, the bad opinion he had formed of them. And so the prince always draws more use from them than from men who, serving him in too much security, neglect his affairs. And since the matter requires it, I will not leave out this reminder to a prince who has newly taken a state by means of inside support from within it: let him weigh well what reason moved the men who supported him to support him. If it was not natural affection for him, but only discontent with the old state, he will keep them friends only with labor and great difficulty, because it will be impossible for him to content them either. Turning over the reason for this in the examples drawn from ancient and modern affairs, he will see that it is far easier to win as friends the men who were content with the old state, and were therefore his enemies, than the men who, being discontent with it, became his friends and helped him seize it.

It has been the custom of princes, the better to hold their states securely, to build fortresses that serve as bridle and bit to those who might design to move against them, and as a safe refuge from a sudden assault. I praise this way of doing things, because it has been used since antiquity. Nevertheless, in our own times Messer Niccolò Vitelli was seen to raze two fortresses in Città di Castello in order to hold that state; Guidobaldo, Duke of Urbino, returning to the dominion Cesare Borgia had driven him from, tore every fortress in that province down to its foundations, judging that without them the state would be harder to lose a second time; and the Bentivogli, returning to Bologna, took similar measures. Fortresses, then, are useful or not according to the times: if they help you in one quarter, they hurt you in another. The question can be put like this: the prince who fears his own people more than foreigners ought to build fortresses; the one who fears foreigners more than his own people ought to leave them alone. The castle of Milan, which Francesco Sforza built there, has made and will make more wars against the house of Sforza than any other disorder in that state. So the best fortress there is, is not to be hated by the people; for though you hold fortresses, if the people hate you the fortresses will not save you — once the people have taken up arms, they never lack for foreigners ready to come to their aid. In our times no fortress can be seen to have profited any prince, except the Countess of Forlì, when her consort Count Girolamo was killed: her fortress let her escape the popular uprising, wait for help from Milan, and recover her state; and the times then stood so that no foreigner could come to the people's aid. But afterward her fortresses too were worth little, when Cesare Borgia attacked her and the people, hostile to her, joined the foreigner. So then, and earlier too, it would have been safer for her not to be hated by the people than to hold the fortresses. Considering all these things, then, I will praise both the prince who builds fortresses and the one who does not; and I will blame any prince who, trusting in fortresses, counts it a small thing to be hated by his people.

Nothing makes a prince so esteemed as great enterprises and rare displays of his own quality. Our own age has Ferdinand of Aragon, the present King of Spain. He can almost be called a new prince, because from a weak king he has become, by fame and glory, the first king in Christendom; and if you examine his deeds you will find them all great, and some of them extraordinary. At the start of his reign he attacked Granada, and that campaign was the foundation of his state. He began it at his leisure and with no fear of interference, for it kept the minds of the barons of Castile fixed on the war and away from any thought of change at home; and meanwhile, without their noticing, he was gaining standing and authority over them. He fed his armies on the money of the Church and of the people, and that long war let him lay a foundation for his own soldiery, which has since brought him honor. Beyond this, always using religion as the pretext for greater designs, he turned to a pious cruelty, hunting the Moors down and clearing them out of his kingdom — no example could be more wretched, or more rare. Under the same cloak he attacked Africa; he made his descent on Italy; he has lately attacked France. So he has never stopped weaving great designs, and they have kept his subjects in suspense and wonder, absorbed in waiting to see how things would come out. And each of his moves has been born out of the last, so that between one and the next, men have never had a quiet stretch in which to work against him.

It also helps a prince a great deal to give rare examples of himself in domestic affairs, like those told of Messer Bernabo da Milano: whenever anyone in civic life did something extraordinary, good or bad, he seized the occasion to reward or punish him in a way that people would talk about for a long time. And above all, a prince must strive in everything he does to earn the name of a great man of exceptional intelligence.

A prince is also esteemed when he is a true friend and a true enemy — when, without hedging, he comes out openly for one side against another. That course is always more useful than standing neutral. For if two of your powerful neighbors come to blows, either the winner will be a threat to you afterward or he will not. In either case it will always be better for you to declare yourself and wage war in earnest. In the first case, if you do not declare yourself, you will be the prize of whoever wins — to the pleasure and satisfaction of whoever loses — and you will have no defense to offer and no reason anyone should give you one, and no one will take you in. The winner does not want doubtful friends who would not stand by him in hard times; the loser will not shelter you, because you would not take up your sword and run his fortune with him.

Antiochus came into Greece, brought in by the Ætolians to drive out the Romans. He sent envoys to the Achaeans, who were friends of the Romans, urging them to stay neutral; the Romans, meanwhile, were urging them to take up arms for their side. The question came before the council of the Achaeans, and when the legate of Antiochus pressed them toward neutrality, the Roman legate answered: “As for the course these men praise as best and most useful for your state — that you keep out of our war — nothing is further from your interest: keep out, and without thanks and without dignity you will be the winner's prize.” So it will always go: the one who is not your friend will ask you for neutrality, and the one who is your friend will ask you to declare yourself with arms. Irresolute princes, trying to escape the danger of the moment, take the neutral road most of the time, and most of the time they are ruined. But when a prince declares himself boldly for one side, then if his ally wins — however powerful the winner, however much you lie at his mercy — he is in your debt; a bond of affection has been formed; and men are never so shameless as to crush you with so flagrant a show of ingratitude. Besides, victories are never so clean that the winner can throw off every restraint, least of all justice. And if your ally loses, he takes you in; while he can, he helps you; and you become companions of a fortune that can rise again.

In the second case, when the two who fight are such that you have nothing to fear from whichever of them wins, it is all the more prudent to take a side: you help destroy the one with the aid of the other, who ought to have rescued him if he had been wise; and since with your help he cannot fail to win, he wins and remains at your discretion. And here it should be noted that a prince ought never to make common cause with someone more powerful than himself in order to attack others, unless necessity forces him, as was said above: for if your stronger partner wins, you are his prisoner, and princes should do all they can to avoid lying at anyone's discretion. The Venetians allied themselves with France against the Duke of Milan — a ruinous alliance they could have avoided. But when it cannot be avoided, as it could not be for the Florentines when the Pope and Spain marched their armies into Lombardy, then the prince should commit himself, for the reasons given.

And let no state ever believe it can choose a safe course; let it expect instead to choose among doubtful ones. For this is in the order of things: you never escape one trouble without walking into another. Prudence consists in knowing how to weigh the troubles against each other, and to take the least bad as good.

A prince should also show himself a lover of excellence, giving a place to able men and honoring those who are outstanding in any art. Beyond that, he should encourage his citizens to follow their occupations in peace — in trade, in farming, in every other human pursuit — so that no one is afraid to improve his property for fear it will be taken from him, and no one afraid to open a business for fear of the taxman. Instead he should hold out rewards for whoever wants to do these things, and for anyone who thinks of any way at all of enlarging his city or his state.

Beyond this, at the fitting seasons of the year, he should keep the people occupied with festivals and spectacles. And since every city is divided into guilds or wards, he should take account of those bodies, meet with them now and then, and show himself in his own person an example of courtesy and generosity — all the while holding the majesty of his rank firm, for that must never be allowed to slip in anything.

The choice of ministers is no small matter for a prince: they are good or not according to the prince's own prudence. The first guess one makes about a ruler's brains comes from seeing the men he keeps around him. When they are capable and faithful, you can always count him wise, because he knew how to recognize their capacity and how to keep them faithful. When they are otherwise, you can always judge him badly, for the first error he made was in this choice.

No one who knew Messer Antonio da Venafro as the minister of Pandolfo Petrucci, prince of Siena, could help judging Pandolfo a most able man for having Venafro as his minister. For there are three kinds of brains: one understands things on its own; the second discerns what others understand; the third understands neither on its own nor through others. The first is most excellent, the second excellent, the third useless. So it necessarily followed that if Pandolfo was not in the first rank, he was in the second: for whenever a man has the judgment to recognize the good and the bad in what another says and does, then even if he has no invention of his own, he can tell his minister's good work from his bad, praise the one and correct the other; and the minister, who cannot hope to fool him, keeps himself good.

But as for how a prince may know his minister, there is a test that never fails. When you see a minister thinking more about himself than about you, and hunting his own profit inside everything he does, a man made that way will never be a good minister, and you will never be able to trust him. For the man who holds another's state in his hands must never think of himself but always of his prince, and must never put before him any business that is not the prince's own.

And on the other side, to keep the minister good, the prince should think of him in turn: honor him, enrich him, bind him with obligations, share the honors and the burdens with him — so that the minister sees he cannot stand without the prince; so that abundant honors leave him wanting no more honors, abundant riches leave him wanting no more riches, and his full load of responsibilities makes him dread any change of regime. When ministers, and princes in their dealings with ministers, are made this way, each can trust the other; and when they are otherwise, it ends badly for one or the other, every time.

I do not want to leave out an important topic, and a mistake princes can hardly defend themselves against unless they are very shrewd, or choose their men very well. I mean the flatterers, and the courts are full of them. For men take such pleasure in their own doings, and deceive themselves about them so thoroughly, that they can barely protect themselves from this plague; and the attempt to protect yourself brings a danger of its own — the danger of becoming despised. There is no way to guard against flattery but to have men understand that telling you the truth does not offend you; yet when everyone may tell you the truth, the reverence goes.

Therefore a prudent prince takes a third way. He chooses wise men from his state, and to them alone he gives free leave to speak the truth to him — and only on the matters he asks about, nothing else. But he should ask them about everything, hear their opinions, and then decide by himself, in his own manner. With these counselors, singly and together, he should carry himself so that every one of them knows the more freely he speaks, the more welcome he will be. Outside of them he should listen to no one, go straight after the thing once decided, and be stubborn in his decisions. Whoever does otherwise is either wrecked by the flatterers, or changes course so often under the pull of contrary opinions that he comes to be despised.

On this point I want to give a modern example. Fra Luca, servant of Maximilian, the present emperor, said of his majesty that he took counsel with no one, and yet never did anything the way he wanted. This came of his doing the opposite of what I have described. For the emperor is a secretive man: he tells no one his plans and takes no advice on them. But as the plans go into effect they begin to show and be discovered, and then the men around him begin to talk him out of them; and he, being pliable, is turned aside. So what he does one day he undoes the next; no one ever understands what he wants or intends to do; and no one can build on his decisions.

A prince, therefore, should always take counsel — but when he wants it, not when others want to give it. In fact he should discourage anyone from volunteering advice on anything unless he asks for it. But he himself should be a generous asker of questions, and then, about the things he asked, a patient hearer of the truth; indeed, when he learns that anyone out of some scruple is keeping the truth from him, he should let his anger show.

Many people suppose that a prince who gives an impression of prudence owes it not to his own nature but to the good advisers around him. They are certainly deceived. For this is a general rule that never fails: a prince who is not wise himself cannot be advised well — unless by chance he hands himself over entirely to a single man of great prudence who governs everything for him. In that case he might indeed be well governed, but it would not last long, because that governor would in short order take the state away from him.

But taking counsel from more than one, a prince who is not wise will never get counsels that agree, and he will not know how to reconcile them himself. Each counselor will think of his own interest; the prince will know neither how to correct them nor how to see through them. And counselors come no other way, because men will always turn out bad for you unless some necessity makes them good. So the conclusion is this: good counsel, wherever it comes from, must be born of the prince's prudence — the prince's prudence is not born of good counsel.

sections.label: Chapter XXIV
sections.title: Why Italy's Princes Lost Their States

segments.text: The measures set out above, prudently observed, make a new prince seem an old one, and settle him faster and more firmly in his state than if he had grown old in it. For a new prince is watched far more closely in his actions than a hereditary one; and when his actions are recognized as able, they take hold of men far more, and bind them far tighter, than ancient blood does. For men are taken much more by present things than by past ones, and when they find the present good they enjoy it and look for nothing else — indeed they will mount every defense of such a prince, so long as he does not fail them in the rest. And so he will have a double glory: to have founded a new principality, and to have adorned and strengthened it with good laws, good arms, good allies, and good examples — just as the man born a prince who loses his state through lack of prudence carries a double shame.

And if you consider the lords who have lost their states in Italy in our times — the King of Naples, the Duke of Milan, and the rest — you will find in them, first, one common defect in the matter of arms, for the causes discussed at length above; and then you will see that some of them either had the people for enemies, or, if they had the people friendly, did not know how to secure the great men. Without these defects, states are not lost that have sinew enough to keep an army in the field.

Philip of Macedon — not Alexander's father, but the one Titus Quintius defeated — did not have much of a state, measured against the greatness of the Romans and of the Greece that attacked him. Yet because he was a military man who knew how to hold the people and secure the great, he sustained the war against them for years; and if in the end he lost his grip on a few cities, the kingdom stayed his.

So let these princes of ours, who held their principalities for years on end and then lost them, blame not fortune but their own laziness. In quiet times they never once considered that things can change — it is the common defect of men not to reckon on the storm while the sea is calm — and when the hard times came, their thoughts ran to flight and not to defense, and they hoped the people, disgusted by the winners' insolence, would call them back. That plan, when all others are gone, is good; but it is very bad to have let the other remedies go for its sake. You should never accept a fall on the faith that someone will be there to pick you up. Either it does not happen, or, if it happens, it brings you no safety — because that kind of rescue is a coward's defense and does not depend on you. The only defenses that are good, that are certain, that are lasting, are the ones that depend on you yourself and on your own strength.

sections.label: Chapter XXV
sections.title: Fortune, and How to Resist Her

segments.text: I am well aware that many men have held, and hold, the opinion that the affairs of the world are so governed by fortune and by God that human prudence cannot correct them — that there is no remedy at all; and on this account they might judge that there is no point sweating over anything, and that we should let ourselves be governed by chance. This opinion has gained more credit in our times because of the great upheavals in affairs that have been seen, and are seen every day, beyond anything anyone could have guessed. Thinking it over, I have myself leaned some way toward their opinion at times. Nevertheless — so that our free will is not extinguished — I judge it may be true that fortune is arbiter of half of our actions, but that she leaves the other half, or close to it, for us to govern.

I compare her to one of those ruinous rivers that, when they grow angry, flood the plains, tear down trees and buildings, lift the earth from this bank and lay it on that one. Everyone flees before the water; everyone gives way to its fury, powerless to stand against it anywhere. And yet, though rivers are made this way, it does not follow that men in quiet weather cannot prepare — with embankments and dikes — so that when the waters rise again they either run off down a channel, or their rush is neither so wild nor so ruinous. It is the same with fortune. She shows her power where no ordered strength stands ready to resist her, and she turns her floods where she knows no dikes and no embankments have been raised to hold her.

And if you consider Italy — the seat of these upheavals, and the country that set them moving — you will see an open plain without dikes and without a single embankment. Had she been protected by proper strength, as Germany, Spain, and France are, either this flood would never have made the great changes it has made, or it would not have come at all. And let this be enough said about resisting fortune in general.

But narrowing myself to particulars, I say that one sees a prince prosper today and fall tomorrow with no visible change in his nature or in any quality he has. This, I believe, comes first from the causes already discussed at length: the prince who leans entirely on fortune falls the moment she turns. I believe, further, that the man prospers who matches his way of proceeding to the quality of the times, and likewise that the man fails whose proceedings are at odds with the times. For in the things that carry men toward the end each one aims at — glory and riches — you see them proceed differently: one with caution, another with a rush; one by force, the other by craft; one by patience, the other by its opposite; and each can arrive by his own road. You also see two cautious men, one reaching his goal and the other not; and again two men prospering equally by opposite methods, one cautious, the other impetuous. All of this comes from nothing but the quality of the times, which either agrees with a man's way of proceeding or does not. From this follows what I said: that two men working differently produce the same effect, and of two working alike, one arrives and the other does not.

On this also hangs the swing of prosperity. If a man governs himself with caution and patience, and times and affairs revolve in a way that makes his method the right one, he prospers; but if times and affairs change, he is ruined, because he does not change his way of proceeding. And no man is found so prudent that he knows how to fit himself to this — both because he cannot swerve from what his own nature inclines him to, and because, having always prospered by walking one road, he cannot be persuaded to leave it. So the cautious man, when the moment comes to strike out, does not know how to do it, and down he goes; whereas if he could change his nature with the times and with affairs, his fortune would not change.

Pope Julius the Second proceeded impetuously in everything he did, and he found the times and circumstances so agreeable to his way of proceeding that things always came out well for him. Consider his first campaign, against Bologna, while Messer Giovanni Bentivogli still lived. The Venetians did not like it; neither did the King of Spain; with France he still had the enterprise under negotiation — and nonetheless, with his usual ferocity and drive, he led the expedition in person. The move left Spain and the Venetians standing frozen, the latter out of fear, the former out of appetite to recover the whole Kingdom of Naples; and at the same time it dragged the King of France in behind him, for the king, seeing him already in motion and wanting the Pope as a friend against the Venetians, judged he could not refuse him troops without an open insult. So with one impetuous stroke Julius accomplished what no other pontiff, with all human prudence, would ever have accomplished. Had he waited in Rome until his plans were settled and everything arranged, as any other pontiff would have done, he would never have succeeded: the King of France would have found a thousand excuses, and the others would have raised a thousand fears.

I will pass over his other deeds, which were all of a piece, and all of them turned out well; and the shortness of his life never let him taste the contrary. For if times had come that required him to proceed with caution, his ruin would have followed: he would never have swerved from the ways his nature inclined him to.

I conclude, then, that since fortune changes and men stand stubborn in their ways, they prosper so long as the two run together, and fail the moment they part. For my own part I judge this: it is better to be impetuous than cautious, because fortune is a woman, and if you mean to keep her down you must beat her and shove her. And plainly she lets herself be won by such men sooner than by those who proceed coldly. And so, like a woman, she is always the friend of the young — because they are less cautious, fiercer, and command her with more audacity.

Having considered everything discussed above, I have been asking myself whether in Italy, right now, the times are ripe to honor a new prince — whether the material lies here that would give a prudent and able man the occasion to shape it into a form that would bring honor to him and good to the whole body of her people. And it seems to me that so many things now run together in a new prince's favor that I do not know what time was ever more fit for one.

If, as I said, the people of Israel had to be slaves in Egypt for the power in Moses to show itself; if the Persians had to be crushed by the Medes for the greatness of Cyrus's spirit to be known, and the Athenians scattered for the excellence of Theseus to appear — then now, for the worth of one Italian spirit to be known, Italy had to be brought down to her present extremity: more enslaved than the Hebrews, more servile than the Persians, more scattered than the Athenians; without a head, without order; beaten, stripped, torn, overrun; made to endure ruin of every kind.

And though before now a glimmer showed in one man, enough to let us think God had ordained him for her redemption, still we saw how afterward, at the very height of his course, fortune cast him off. So she lies there as if lifeless, waiting for whoever it may be that can heal her wounds — put an end to the sacking of Lombardy, to the extortion of the kingdom and of Tuscany — and clean out the sores that have festered now for so long. See how she prays God to send someone to redeem her from these cruelties and this barbarian insolence. See how ready she is, how willing, to march behind a flag — if only someone would raise one.

Nor is there anyone now in view in whom she can place more hope than in your illustrious house, which — with its fortune and its ability, favored by God and by the Church, of which it is now the head — can make itself the leader of this redemption. That will not be very hard if you hold before your eyes the deeds and the lives of the men named above. They were rare and marvelous men; but they were men, and none of them had an opportunity as good as this one: their enterprise was not more just than this, nor easier, nor was God more a friend to them than he is to you.

Here justice is great: for war is just for those to whom it is necessary, and arms are holy where there is no hope left except in arms. Here the willingness is very great; and where the willingness is great, the difficulty cannot be great, provided your house takes as its mark the methods of the men I have held up. Beyond this, extraordinary things without precedent have been seen here, God leading the way: the sea has opened; a cloud has shown the road; the rock has poured out water; manna has rained down. Everything has run together toward your greatness. The rest you must do yourselves. God does not want to do everything, lest he take from us our free will and the share of the glory that falls to us.

And it is no wonder if none of the Italians named before could do what we may hope from your illustrious house, or if in so many revolutions and so many campaigns of war in Italy it always looks as if military virtue were spent. The truth is that her old institutions were bad, and no one has appeared who knew how to find new ones. Nothing brings a newly risen man so much honor as the new laws and new institutions he devises: when they are well founded and have greatness in them, they make him revered and admired. And in Italy the material is not lacking — it will take any form you can give it.

Here there is great strength in the limbs, if only it were not missing in the heads. Look at the duels and the small combats: how superior the Italians are in strength, in dexterity, in quickness of wit. But when it comes to armies they make no showing. And all of it traces back to the weakness of the heads: the men who know are not obeyed, every man thinks he knows, and no one until now has known how to lift himself, by ability or by fortune, so far above the rest that the others would yield to him. That is why, over so long a time, through so many wars in the past twenty years, whenever an army has been all Italian it has always failed the test. The first witness is Il Taro; then Allesandria, Capua, Genoa, Vaila, Bologna, Mestri.

If your illustrious house, then, means to follow those excellent men who redeemed their countries, one thing is necessary before all others, the true foundation of every such enterprise: to arm yourself with your own troops, for there can be no more faithful, truer, or better soldiers. And good as each man of them is singly, together they will be better still when they see themselves commanded by their own prince, honored by him, and kept at his charge. These arms must be prepared, so that with Italian strength we can defend ourselves against the foreigner.

The Swiss and the Spanish infantry are counted terrifying, it is true; yet each has a defect, so that a third order of troops could not only stand against them but be confident of beating them. For the Spaniards cannot withstand cavalry, and the Swiss have reason to fear infantry that meets them in close combat as stubbornly as they fight. So we have seen, and will see again by experience, that the Spaniards cannot hold against French cavalry, and the Swiss are broken by Spanish infantry. Of this last there is no complete proof yet, but a taste of it was given at the battle of Ravenna, when the Spanish infantry met the German battalions, which keep the same order as the Swiss: the Spaniards, with the agility of their bodies and the help of their bucklers, got in under the Germans' pikes and stood there safe, cutting at them while the Germans had no remedy; and had the cavalry not charged them, the Spaniards would have finished them all. Knowing the defect of both these infantries, then, one can order a new kind, able to stand against horse and unafraid of foot — and this will be done by the kind of arms chosen and a change of formations. These are among the things which, ordered fresh, give reputation and greatness to a new prince.

This opportunity, then, must not be let slip, so that Italy, after so long, may at last see her redeemer. I cannot express with what love he would be received in all the provinces that have suffered these foreign floods; with what thirst for vengeance, what stubborn faith, what devotion, what tears. What doors would be shut against him? What people would refuse him obedience? What envy would set itself against him? What Italian would withhold his homage? To every one of us this barbarian rule stinks. Let your illustrious house take up this cause, then, with the spirit and the hope in which just enterprises are taken up; so that under its banner this country may be made noble again, and under its auspices Petrarch's words may come true:
Virtù contro al Furore prenderà l'arme, e fia il combatter corto: ché l'antico valore negli italici cuor non è ancor morto.
Virtue against fury will take up arms; and the fight will be short: for the ancient valor in Italian hearts is not yet dead.
